**Lecture 1 Computers, files, OS, command line**

*Year 1 · Month 1 · Computer, Data & Python Foundations · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
|-------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Explain, in plain terms, what the CPU, RAM, and storage each do inside a computer and why that split matters for running code.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
| **Teacher explanation** | A computer separates fast, volatile working memory (RAM) from slow, persistent storage (SSD/HDD), with the CPU fetching instructions and data from RAM and executing them one step at a time. When you double-click a program, the operating system copies its code from storage into RAM so the CPU can run it; close the program and RAM is freed, but files on disk stay put until you delete them. This is why a Python script that 'runs out of memory' is a RAM problem, not a storage problem, and why saving your work to a file is what protects it from a crash or power loss. The operating system (Windows, macOS, Linux) is the layer that mediates all of this: it schedules which program gets the CPU next, and it manages which process can read or write which files. We will use this model all month: every time you run a script, picture the OS loading it into RAM and the CPU stepping through it line by line. |
| **Worked example**      | Open your system's Task Manager (Windows) or Activity Monitor (macOS) and find three numbers: CPU % in use, RAM used/total, and disk free space. Open a text editor, type a sentence, and watch RAM usage tick up slightly (bytes in memory) while disk usage does not change until you hit Save (bytes written to storage).                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |

**Knowledge check:** A program is launched and runs noticeably slowly, then the OS reports available RAM is nearly zero. What is the most likely explanation?

\(A\) The CPU clock speed has stopped

**(B) The program and its data cannot all stay in fast working memory at once, so the system is swapping data to slower disk storage**

\(C\) The storage drive is full

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** On your own machine, note the total RAM installed and the free disk space, then list which of your five most-used applications you would guess uses the most RAM and why.

**Lecture 2 Computers, files, OS, command line**

*Year 1 · Month 1 · Computer, Data & Python Foundations · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
|-------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Describe how a file system organizes files into a tree of directories and construct both absolute and relative paths to a file.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| **Teacher explanation** | A file system is a tree: a single root (C:\\ on Windows, / on macOS/Linux) with directories (folders) branching off it, and files living at the tips of branches. An absolute path writes the full route from the root, e.g. /Users/dana/projects/data.csv or C:\Users\Dana\projects\data.csv, and it works no matter where you currently are. A relative path is written from your current location (the 'working directory'): if you are already inside /Users/dana/projects, then just data.csv or ./data.csv refers to the same file, and ../ means 'go up one directory.' Mixing these up is the single most common beginner bug — a script that works on your machine can fail on a classmate's because it hard-codes an absolute path that does not exist on their computer. We will practice building both kinds of paths by hand before touching any code that opens a file. |
| **Worked example**      | Given the tree projects/ containing data/raw_sales.csv and scripts/clean.py, write the relative path from scripts/clean.py to raw_sales.csv: it is ../data/raw_sales.csv, because you must step up out of scripts/ before stepping down into data/.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |

**Knowledge check:** You are currently inside the folder /home/dana/project/scripts. Which path correctly refers to a file named input.csv sitting in /home/dana/project/data?

\(A\) ./input.csv

**(B) ../data/input.csv**

\(C\) /scripts/data/input.csv

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Draw (on paper or in a text file) the actual folder tree of one real project on your computer, at least three levels deep, and write both the absolute and relative path to one file in it.

**Lecture 3 Computers, files, OS, command line**

*Year 1 · Month 1 · Computer, Data & Python Foundations · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
|-------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Navigate a file system from the command line using pwd, ls/dir, cd, mkdir, and cp/mv without using a graphical file explorer.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
| **Teacher explanation** | The command line is a text interface to the same file tree you see in a graphical explorer, just faster once you know the verbs. pwd (print working directory) tells you where you are; ls (macOS/Linux) or dir (Windows) lists what is in that directory; cd folder_name moves you into it, and cd .. moves you up one level. mkdir new_folder creates a directory, cp source destination copies a file (copy-item on Windows PowerShell), and mv source destination moves or renames it. Every one of these commands is just manipulating the same tree structure you learned in the previous lecture — there is no separate 'command line file system,' only a different way to point at the same paths. We will run a sequence of these commands live to build a small project folder from scratch. |
| **Worked example**      | Starting from an empty folder, the sequence: mkdir project, cd project, mkdir data scripts, cd data, (place a file test.csv here), cd ../scripts produces the same two-folder layout you could have built by right-clicking in a GUI — but it is scriptable and repeatable.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |

**Knowledge check:** You run \`cd data\` and then immediately run \`cd data\` again. What happens?

\(A\) Nothing changes, you stay in the same place

\(B\) You move up one level back to where you started

**(C) You get an error, because there is no data folder inside data (unless one actually exists)**

***Correct answer: C***

**Homework:** Using only the terminal, create a folder called week1, move into it, create two subfolders named raw and clean, and copy any one file from elsewhere on your computer into raw.

**Lecture 4 Computers, files, OS, command line**

*Year 1 · Month 1 · Computer, Data & Python Foundations · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
|-------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Diagnose and fix the most common command-line mistakes: wrong working directory, mistyped paths, and missing permissions.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
| **Teacher explanation** | Three error types account for most beginner command-line failures. 'No such file or directory' almost always means your path is wrong relative to pwd — check where you are before blaming the command. 'Permission denied' means the operating system's file permissions block your user from reading/writing/executing that file or folder; on macOS/Linux this is visible via ls -l as a string like -rw-r--r--, and fixed (carefully) with chmod. 'Command not found' means the program you typed is not installed or not on your PATH — the list of folders the shell searches when you type a command name. We will deliberately trigger all three errors and read the exact wording the terminal gives, because learning to read an error message precisely is a bigger skill gain than memorizing commands. |
| **Worked example**      | Typing \`cd dektop\` (a typo for Desktop) produces 'No such file or directory: dektop' — the fix is not a new command, it's correcting the spelling and matching the exact case the OS uses (case-sensitive on Linux, usually not on Windows/macOS).                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |

**Knowledge check:** Running a command gives you exactly: \`bash: foo.sh: Permission denied\`. What is the most direct fix?

\(A\) Reinstall the operating system

**(B) Make the file executable, e.g. with chmod +x foo.sh, then run it again**

\(C\) Rename the file to remove special characters

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Intentionally trigger a 'No such file or directory' error and a 'command not found' error on your machine, and write down the exact fix for each.

**Lecture 5 Computers, files, OS, command line**

*Year 1 · Month 1 · Computer, Data & Python Foundations · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
|-------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Write and run a short shell script that automates a sequence of file operations you previously typed by hand.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
| **Teacher explanation** | A shell script is just a text file of the same commands you've been typing, run in order when you execute the file instead of retyping each line. On macOS/Linux you write lines like mkdir backup, cp data.csv backup/, save as setup.sh, make it executable with chmod +x setup.sh, and run it with ./setup.sh; on Windows you'd write the PowerShell equivalents in a .ps1 file. This is the first real taste of automation: the same five commands that took you thirty seconds to type by hand now run in under a second, identically, every time. This matters because every data pipeline you build for the rest of this course is, underneath, a sequence of exactly this kind of scripted step — read a file, transform it, write a new file. We close the week by tying together paths (lecture 2), navigation commands (lecture 3), and error-reading (lecture 4) into one working script. |
| **Worked example**      | A three-line script: \`mkdir -p archive\`, \`cp \*.csv archive/\`, \`echo "backup complete"\` — run once, it creates an archive folder, copies every CSV in the current folder into it, and prints a confirmation, replacing four manual steps with one command.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |

**Knowledge check:** Why is a shell script more reliable than typing the same five commands by hand each time?

\(A\) It runs on a different, faster processor

**(B) It executes the exact same sequence every time with no risk of typos or skipped steps**

\(C\) It does not require a working directory

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Write a shell script of at least three commands that sets up a standard project folder structure (e.g. data/, scripts/, output/), then run it twice in two different empty locations to confirm it works identically both times.

**Lecture 6 what data is**

*Year 1 · Month 1 · Computer, Data & Python Foundations · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
|-------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Distinguish quantitative from qualitative data and discrete from continuous quantitative data, with examples of each.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
| **Teacher explanation** | Data splits first into quantitative (numeric, measuring 'how much' or 'how many') and qualitative (categorical, describing 'what kind'). Quantitative data further splits into discrete — countable whole units like number of orders or number of children, which can never be a fraction — and continuous, like height or temperature, which can take any value in a range and is limited only by how precisely you measure it. Qualitative data splits into nominal, where categories have no natural order (e.g. payment method: cash/card/transfer), and ordinal, where they do (e.g. customer satisfaction: low/medium/high). Getting this classification right matters immediately and practically: it determines which statistics are even valid later — you can average a continuous column but averaging a nominal column like 'city' is meaningless. |
| **Worked example**      | In a retail dataset with columns order_id, num_items, delivery_time_hours, and payment_method: num_items is discrete quantitative (always a whole number), delivery_time_hours is continuous quantitative (can be 2.37 hours), and payment_method is nominal qualitative (no inherent order among cash/card/transfer).                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |

**Knowledge check:** Which of the following is continuous quantitative data?

\(A\) Number of items purchased in an order

**(B) Weight of a package in kilograms**

\(C\) Customer-selected shipping speed: slow/standard/fast

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Pick any spreadsheet or dataset you have access to and label each column as discrete, continuous, nominal, or ordinal, justifying each label in one sentence.

**Lecture 7 what data is**

*Year 1 · Month 1 · Computer, Data & Python Foundations · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
|-------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Explain the difference between structured, semi-structured, and unstructured data, and identify real examples of each.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| **Teacher explanation** | Structured data fits neatly into rows and columns with a fixed schema known in advance — a spreadsheet of sales transactions or a SQL table are the clearest examples. Semi-structured data has some organizing tags or keys but no rigid row/column shape, such as a JSON object or an email with a header and a free-text body — the structure is there, but it is flexible and can nest. Unstructured data has no predefined organization at all: a photograph, an audio recording, or a block of free-text customer reviews. The amount of work needed before you can analyze data rises sharply across this spectrum: structured data might need only filtering, semi-structured data needs parsing/flattening, and unstructured data typically needs a whole separate extraction step (e.g. NLP to turn review text into sentiment scores) before it resembles structured data at all. |
| **Worked example**      | A customer support system stores: a structured ticket table (ticket_id, date, status columns), a semi-structured JSON log of each ticket's event history ({"event":"opened","ts":...}), and unstructured free-text messages the customer typed — all three describing the same support ticket, at three different structure levels.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |

**Knowledge check:** A JSON file where each record has keys like name, email, and an optional nested 'addresses' list (some records have it, some don't, and the list can be any length) is best classified as:

\(A\) Structured data

**(B) Semi-structured data**

\(C\) Unstructured data

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Find one real example on your own computer or email of each of the three types (structured, semi-structured, unstructured) and write one sentence on what would need to happen before each could be loaded into a spreadsheet.

**Lecture 8 what data is**

*Year 1 · Month 1 · Computer, Data & Python Foundations · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
|-------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Trace how data commonly reaches an organization — flat files, databases, and APIs — and state one tradeoff of each source.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| **Teacher explanation** | Flat files (CSV, Excel, TXT) are the simplest data source: easy to open and share, but there is no built-in way to query them efficiently or enforce that every row has valid data, so a 10-million-row CSV is slow and error-prone. A database (like PostgreSQL or MySQL) stores data with enforced structure and lets you query exactly the rows and columns you need via SQL, but someone has to design the schema and maintain the server. An API (Application Programming Interface) lets you request live data over the internet in a defined format (usually JSON) — e.g. pulling today's currency exchange rate — trading the simplicity of a file for freshness, at the cost of needing network access and handling rate limits or downtime. Most real data-analyst work touches all three in the same week: exporting a flat file from a vendor, querying the company database, and calling an API for live context. |
| **Worked example**      | A sales analyst gets last year's archived transactions as a CSV emailed by finance (flat file), queries this month's live transactions from the production database (database), and calls a public API to pull current exchange rates needed to convert foreign sales to USD (API) — three different sources feeding one analysis.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |

**Knowledge check:** What is the main disadvantage of a flat CSV file compared to a database for a 10-million-row dataset?

\(A\) CSV files cannot store numbers

**(B) Querying and filtering efficiently is much harder; the whole file typically must be loaded before you can select just what you need**

\(C\) CSV files cannot be opened on Windows

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** List the data sources you have personally touched in the last month (files, apps, websites) and classify each as a flat file, a database-backed system, or an API-driven feed.

**Lecture 9 what data is**

*Year 1 · Month 1 · Computer, Data & Python Foundations · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
|-------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Identify common data quality problems — missing values, duplicates, and inconsistent formatting — in a small sample dataset.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
| **Teacher explanation** | Missing values appear as blanks, NULL, NaN, or sometimes a disguised placeholder like 999 or 'N/A' typed into a numeric field — and the danger is that undetected missing data silently skews any average or count you compute. Duplicates occur when the same real-world event is recorded more than once, often because of a failed retry in a data pipeline or a copy-paste error, and they inflate totals and counts if not removed. Inconsistent formatting is the quiet killer: 'NY', 'New York', and 'new york' are the same city to a human but three different strings to software, and a date stored as 03/04/2026 is ambiguous between March 4th and April 3rd depending on locale. Before any analysis, a careful look for these three issues — usually by sorting, counting unique values, and scanning a sample — prevents wrong conclusions later in the course. |
| **Worked example**      | A customer_city column containing 'NYC', 'New York', 'new york city', and 'NY' is really one category split four ways by inconsistent formatting; counting unique values on this column before cleaning would wrongly suggest four different, smaller cities instead of one large one.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |

**Knowledge check:** A dataset of 10,000 customer rows has 10,050 rows after an import. What data quality issue does this most likely indicate?

\(A\) Missing values

**(B) Duplicate records**

\(C\) Inconsistent date formatting

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Open any dataset (even a short spreadsheet you create with 15 rows) and deliberately introduce one missing value, one duplicate row, and one inconsistently formatted text entry — then write one sentence describing how you would spot each if you did not already know where they were.

**Lecture 10 what data is**

*Year 1 · Month 1 · Computer, Data & Python Foundations · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
|-------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Build a simple data dictionary that documents each column of a small dataset: its name, type, meaning, and valid range.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| **Teacher explanation** | A data dictionary is a short reference document, usually a table, listing every column in a dataset alongside its data type, a plain-language description of what it means, and any constraints (e.g. age must be between 0 and 120, status must be one of 'active'/'inactive'/'pending'). It exists because a column name alone is often ambiguous — does 'amount' mean before or after tax, in dollars or cents? — and because the person analyzing data is frequently not the person who collected it. Writing one forces you to notice ambiguities and quality issues (from the previous lecture) before they cause a wrong conclusion, and it is standard practice at every real data team, often stored alongside the dataset itself or in a shared wiki. This lecture is the synthesis of the week: you'll apply the classification skills from lecture 6, the source awareness from lecture 8, and the quality checks from lecture 9 into one finished artifact. |
| **Worked example**      | For a column named amt_cents in an orders table, a data dictionary entry reads: Name: amt_cents \| Type: integer (discrete quantitative) \| Meaning: total order value in US cents, pre-tax \| Valid range: 0 to 10,000,000 (i.e. up to \$100,000) \| Notes: never negative; a negative value indicates a refund record and should be flagged.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |

**Knowledge check:** Why is a data dictionary useful even when the column names seem self-explanatory, like 'price'?

\(A\) It is required by law in every country

**(B) It removes the ambiguity that column names alone leave open, such as currency, units, tax inclusion, and valid ranges**

\(C\) It automatically fixes missing values in the dataset

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Choose a small dataset (5+ columns) and write a complete data dictionary entry for every column, including at least one constraint or valid range per column.

**Lecture 11 variables, types and basic Python**

*Year 1 · Month 1 · Computer, Data & Python Foundations · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
|-------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Create Python variables holding int, float, str, and bool values, and name them following Python's naming conventions.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               |
| **Teacher explanation** | A variable is a named label pointing at a value stored in memory; in Python you create one with a single assignment statement like age = 29, with no separate declaration step required, because Python infers the type from the value itself. The four core built-in types you'll use constantly are int (whole numbers, age = 29), float (decimals, price = 19.99), str (text, wrapped in quotes, name = "Dana"), and bool (True or False, is_active = True). Python naming convention (PEP 8) says variable names use lowercase with underscores (snake_case, e.g. total_price, not TotalPrice or totalPrice), must start with a letter or underscore, and cannot be a reserved word like class or if. Getting the type right matters immediately: Python will let you write age = "29" (a string that looks like a number) and that silent mistake causes real bugs the moment you try to do arithmetic with it. |
| **Worked example**      | price = 19.99 creates a float; you can confirm this by running type(price), which prints \<class 'float'\>; running type("19.99") on the quoted version instead prints \<class 'str'\>, demonstrating that quotes alone change the type regardless of what the text looks like.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |

**Knowledge check:** What type does Python assign to the variable created by \`count = 5\`?

\(A\) str

**(B) int**

\(C\) float

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** In a new Python file, create one variable of each of the four core types (int, float, str, bool) with names following snake_case, and print each one's value together with its type using the type() function.

**Lecture 12 variables, types and basic Python**

*Year 1 · Month 1 · Computer, Data & Python Foundations · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               |
|-------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Convert values between types using int(), float(), str(), and bool(), and explain when each conversion can fail or surprise you.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
| **Teacher explanation** | Type conversion (casting) lets you move a value from one type to another: int("42") turns the string "42" into the integer 42, float("3.14") turns a string into a decimal, and str(42) turns a number back into text for display or concatenation. These conversions are not symmetric in difficulty: int("42") works, but int("forty-two") raises a ValueError because Python cannot parse that text as a number, and int(3.9) truncates toward zero to 3 rather than rounding, which surprises many beginners expecting 4. bool() conversion has its own quirks worth memorizing: bool(0), bool(""), bool(\[\]), and bool(None) are all False, while almost everything else, including bool("False") (a non-empty string!), is True. We will deliberately run several of these edge cases live so you see the error messages and surprising outputs before they bite you in a real script. |
| **Worked example**      | Running int("7.5") raises ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: '7.5' — because int() cannot parse a decimal point directly from a string; the fix is to go through float first: int(float("7.5")) gives 7.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |

**Knowledge check:** What does bool("False") evaluate to in Python, and why?

\(A\) False, because the text says False

**(B) True, because any non-empty string is truthy regardless of its content**

\(C\) It raises an error, because 'False' is not a valid boolean literal

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Write five short lines of code that each attempt a type conversion likely to surprise a beginner (e.g. int(3.9), bool("0"), int("3.5")), run them, and write one sentence per line explaining the actual output.

**Lecture 13 variables, types and basic Python**

*Year 1 · Month 1 · Computer, Data & Python Foundations · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
|-------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Use Python's arithmetic and comparison operators correctly, including the differences between / and //, and == and =.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               |
| **Teacher explanation** | Python's arithmetic operators are +, -, \*, / (true division, always returns a float, e.g. 7/2 is 3.5), // (floor division, discards the remainder, 7//2 is 3), and % (modulo, the remainder itself, 7%2 is 1). A single = is assignment (it stores a value into a variable), while == is the comparison operator that checks equality and returns a bool — confusing these two is one of the most common syntax bugs beginners write, and Python will raise a SyntaxError if you try to use = inside a condition like if x = 5:. Comparison operators (==, !=, \<, \>, \<=, \>=) always return True or False and are the building blocks of every conditional and loop you will write for the rest of the course. We build a small temperature converter this lecture specifically to force correct use of both arithmetic (the conversion formula) and the distinction between = and == when checking the result. |
| **Worked example**      | Converting 100 degrees Celsius to Fahrenheit: fahrenheit = celsius \* 9/5 + 32 gives fahrenheit = 212.0; checking the result with fahrenheit == 212 compares the stored value to the literal 212 and returns True, while writing fahrenheit = 212 by mistake would silently overwrite your computed result with a constant.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |

**Knowledge check:** What does the expression 17 // 5 evaluate to in Python?

\(A\) 3.4

\(B\) 2

**(C) 3**

***Correct answer: C***

**Homework:** Write a temperature converter script that takes a Celsius value, computes Fahrenheit using the correct formula, and prints a sentence confirming the result using an == comparison against the expected value for one known test case (0°C should equal 32°F).

**Lecture 14 variables, types and basic Python**

*Year 1 · Month 1 · Computer, Data & Python Foundations · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
|-------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Debug the most common type-related errors beginners hit: TypeError from mixing str and int, and off-by-one indexing mistakes.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
| **Teacher explanation** | TypeError: can only concatenate str (not "int") to str is the single most frequent early error, produced by code like print("Age: " + age) when age is an int — Python's + operator refuses to silently convert types, unlike some languages, and the fix is either str(age) or an f-string like f"Age: {age}". A second very common family of bugs involves string and list indexing being zero-based: the first character of "hello" is "hello"\[0\] (which is 'h'), not "hello"\[1\], and "hello"\[5\] raises IndexError: string index out of range because valid indices only run from 0 to len-1 (here, 0 to 4). We will read several real Python tracebacks line by line in this lecture, because learning to locate the actual failing line (usually the last one shown) and the actual error type (the word before the colon) is a transferable debugging skill, not a Python-specific one. By the end you should be able to predict, before running the code, whether a given line will raise TypeError, IndexError, or ValueError. |
| **Worked example**      | Code \`name = "Dana"; print("Hi " + name + ", you are " + 29)\` raises TypeError on the last concatenation because 29 is an int; changing it to str(29) or rewriting the whole line as an f-string f"Hi {name}, you are 29" both fix it, but the f-string version also reads more clearly.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |

**Knowledge check:** What is the correct zero-based index to retrieve the letter 'o' from the string "hello"?

\(A\) 3

**(B) 4**

\(C\) 5

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Take three lines of broken code you write on purpose (one causing TypeError, one causing IndexError, one causing ValueError), run each, copy the exact error message, and write the one-line fix for each.

**Lecture 15 variables, types and basic Python**

*Year 1 · Month 1 · Computer, Data & Python Foundations · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
|-------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Combine variables, types, conversions, and operators into a working multi-step calculator script that takes input and prints a formatted result.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
| **Teacher explanation** | This lecture's script collects a numeric input with Python's input() function (which always returns a str, so it must be converted with float() or int() before arithmetic — tying directly back to lecture 12), performs a calculation using the correct operators from lecture 13, and prints a clearly formatted result using an f-string, avoiding the str/int TypeError from lecture 14. A realistic example is a simple tip calculator: read the bill amount and the tip percentage as text input, convert both to float, multiply to get the tip, add it to the bill for the total, and print all three figures rounded to two decimal places with round(value, 2). This is deliberately the first script in the course that chains every skill from the week — variable creation, type conversion, arithmetic, and string formatting — into one coherent, runnable program rather than an isolated demonstration of one concept. Finishing this script successfully is good evidence you are ready for Month 1's examination. |
| **Worked example**      | bill = float(input("Bill amount: ")); tip_pct = float(input("Tip %: ")); tip = round(bill \* tip_pct / 100, 2); total = round(bill + tip, 2); print(f"Tip: \${tip}, Total: \${total}") — running it with bill=50 and tip_pct=20 prints Tip: \$10.0, Total: \$60.0.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |

**Knowledge check:** In the calculator script, why must float(input(...)) be used instead of just input(...) directly in the arithmetic?

**(A) input() returns a string, and arithmetic operators like \* will fail or behave incorrectly on strings**

\(B\) input() only works with integers, never decimals

\(C\) float() is required to print the result

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Extend the tip calculator to also ask for the number of people splitting the bill and print each person's share, rounded to two decimal places, ready to demo in the Month 1 exam review.

**Lecture 17 Functions**

*Year 1 · Month 2 · Python Programming for Data · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
|-------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
