|-------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Apply UMAP for faster, more structure-preserving 2D embeddings and contrast feature extraction with feature selection.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
| **Teacher explanation** | UMAP (Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection) is, like t-SNE, a nonlinear embedding technique for visualization and preprocessing, but it is built on manifold learning theory and typically runs much faster and scales to larger datasets, while tending to preserve more of the global structure (relative positions of distinct clusters) alongside local neighborhoods. Its two main hyperparameters are n_neighbors (how many neighbors define the local manifold around each point — small values emphasize fine local detail, large values emphasize broader structure) and min_dist (how tightly points are allowed to pack together in the embedding — small values produce tighter, more clumped clusters). This lecture also draws the line between dimensionality reduction methods that are feature extraction (PCA, t-SNE, UMAP — they create new axes that are combinations of all original features, so the originals are no longer individually interpretable) versus feature selection (choosing a subset of the ORIGINAL features to keep, e.g. by variance threshold or mutual information with a target) — feature selection keeps interpretability, extraction maximizes information compression. |
| **Worked example**      | import umap reducer = umap.UMAP(n_neighbors=15, min_dist=0.1, random_state=0) emb = reducer.fit_transform(Xs) \# contrast with feature selection: from sklearn.feature_selection import VarianceThreshold selected = VarianceThreshold(threshold=0.01).fit_transform(Xs) print(Xs.shape, emb.shape, selected.shape)                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |

**Knowledge check:** What fundamentally distinguishes feature selection from feature extraction methods like PCA or UMAP?

**(A) Feature selection keeps a subset of the original, interpretable features; feature extraction creates new combined axes from all original features**

\(B\) Feature extraction is only usable on labeled data, feature selection only on unlabeled data

\(C\) There is no real difference; the terms are interchangeable

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Run UMAP on the same dataset you used for t-SNE with n_neighbors=5 and n_neighbors=50, compare the two embeddings, and list one feature-selection method you could use instead if interpretability of the original columns mattered.

**Lecture 269 dimensionality reduction concepts**

*Year 2 · Month 16 · Unsupervised Learning · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
|-------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Compare PCA, t-SNE, and UMAP embeddings side by side on the same high-dimensional dataset and interpret what each reveals.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
| **Teacher explanation** | This worked example takes a genuinely high-dimensional dataset (for example, Fashion-MNIST pixel vectors, 784 features per image, or a gene-expression matrix with hundreds of columns) and reduces it to 2D three different ways — PCA, t-SNE, and UMAP — so the differences are visible rather than theoretical. PCA's plot typically shows a loose, somewhat overlapping cloud because it's constrained to linear projections and optimizes for variance, not class separation. The t-SNE and UMAP plots typically show much tighter, more visually separated groupings of same-label points, because both are nonlinear and explicitly optimize for preserving neighborhood structure — but as established in lecture 267, that visual tightness should not be read as a precise distance metric. The practical takeaway for a working data scientist: use PCA first (it's fast, deterministic, and useful for noise reduction or as a preprocessing step before clustering or modeling); use t-SNE/UMAP for exploratory visualization when you want to eyeball whether classes or clusters are separable at all. |
| **Worked example**      | from sklearn.decomposition import PCA from sklearn.manifold import TSNE import umap Xs = StandardScaler().fit_transform(X) \# e.g. a sample of Fashion-MNIST pca_emb = PCA(n_components=2).fit_transform(Xs) tsne_emb = TSNE(n_components=2, random_state=0).fit_transform(Xs) umap_emb = umap.UMAP(random_state=0).fit_transform(Xs) \# plot all three side-by-side, colored by true label, and compare visual separation                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |

**Knowledge check:** Why does a PCA 2D plot of a complex dataset often look less visually separated by class than a t-SNE or UMAP plot of the same data?

\(A\) PCA is buggy and should not be used on complex datasets

**(B) PCA is restricted to linear projections optimizing for overall variance, while t-SNE/UMAP use nonlinear transforms explicitly optimized to preserve local neighborhood/class structure**

\(C\) PCA always requires more components than 2 to work correctly

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Take a dataset with at least 50 features and a known label column, produce PCA, t-SNE, and UMAP 2D plots colored by that label, and write two sentences comparing how well each method visually separates the classes.

**Lecture 270 dimensionality reduction concepts**

*Year 2 · Month 16 · Unsupervised Learning · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
|-------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Avoid the standard dimensionality-reduction mistakes and build a PCA-preprocessing pipeline that feeds into a downstream clustering or classification step.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
| **Teacher explanation** | The most common dimensionality-reduction mistakes are: fitting PCA on unscaled data (letting high-magnitude features dominate the components), choosing n_components arbitrarily instead of by a cumulative-variance threshold or downstream validation performance, applying t-SNE/UMAP output as if the axes had intrinsic meaning (they don't — the axes are not the original features and aren't comparable across separate runs), and fitting PCA separately on train and test sets (causing train/test feature-space mismatch; you must fit PCA on training data only and use .transform() on the test set). This lecture builds a correct pipeline: StandardScaler -\> PCA (fit on train, transform both) -\> downstream estimator (e.g. KMeans or a classifier), wrapped in a scikit-learn Pipeline so the fitting order is enforced automatically and cross-validation folds get consistent treatment. It also covers PCA's inverse_transform for approximate reconstruction, which is a direct, visual way to show how much information was lost at a given n_components. |
| **Worked example**      | from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler from sklearn.decomposition import PCA from sklearn.cluster import KMeans pipe = Pipeline(\[ ('scale', StandardScaler()), ('pca', PCA(n_components=0.90)), \# keep enough components for 90% variance ('cluster', KMeans(n_clusters=4, n_init=10, random_state=0)) \]) labels = pipe.fit_predict(X_train) \# reconstruction error check: Xr = pipe.named_steps\['pca'\].inverse_transform(pipe.named_steps\['pca'\].transform(pipe.named_steps\['scale'\].transform(X_test)))                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |

**Knowledge check:** What is wrong with fitting PCA separately on the training set and separately on the test set?

\(A\) Nothing, this is the recommended approach

**(B) It creates two different, incompatible component spaces, so features extracted from train and test data are no longer comparable to each other**

\(C\) PCA cannot be fit on a test set under any circumstances

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Build a scikit-learn Pipeline that scales, applies PCA with n_components=0.90, and fits KMeans; fit it on a train split and report cluster assignments and reconstruction error on a held-out test split.

**Lecture 271 anomaly detection**

*Year 2 · Month 16 · Unsupervised Learning · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               |
|-------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Detect univariate outliers using z-scores and the IQR rule, and explain when each assumption breaks down.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| **Teacher explanation** | The simplest anomaly-detection methods work on a single feature at a time. The z-score method assumes the feature is roughly normally distributed and flags any point where \|z\| = \|(x - mean) / std\| exceeds a threshold, commonly 3 — meaning the point is more than 3 standard deviations from the mean. The IQR (interquartile range) method makes no normality assumption: it computes Q1 (25th percentile) and Q3 (75th percentile), IQR = Q3 - Q1, and flags anything below Q1 - 1.5\*IQR or above Q3 + 1.5\*IQR (the same rule a boxplot's whiskers use), making it more robust to skewed distributions and to the outliers themselves inflating the mean/std used by the z-score method. Both methods only look at one column at a time, so they will miss a 'contextual' or 'multivariate' anomaly — a point that's unremarkable on every single feature individually but unusual in how those features combine (e.g. a 'normal' age combined with a 'normal' income that together are implausible, like a toddler earning a six-figure salary). |
| **Worked example**      | import numpy as np x = df\['transaction_amount'\] z = (x - x.mean()) / x.std() outliers_z = df\[z.abs() \> 3\] Q1, Q3 = x.quantile(0.25), x.quantile(0.75) IQR = Q3 - Q1 outliers_iqr = df\[(x \< Q1 - 1.5\*IQR) \| (x \> Q3 + 1.5\*IQR)\] print(len(outliers_z), len(outliers_iqr))                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |

**Knowledge check:** Why is the IQR method often preferred over the z-score method for skewed data with extreme outliers?

\(A\) IQR is always faster to compute

**(B) The z-score method relies on the mean and standard deviation, both of which are themselves distorted by extreme outliers, whereas IQR uses robust quantiles**

\(C\) IQR requires labeled anomaly data while z-score does not

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** On a numeric column of your choice, compute outliers via both the z-score (threshold 3) and IQR (1.5x) rules, compare how many points each method flags, and explain any difference you see.

**Lecture 272 anomaly detection**

*Year 2 · Month 16 · Unsupervised Learning · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               |
|-------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Train an Isolation Forest and interpret its anomaly scores for multivariate outlier detection.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
| **Teacher explanation** | Isolation Forest flips the usual density-based intuition: instead of modeling what 'normal' looks like, it exploits the fact that anomalies are 'few and different', so they are easier to isolate. It builds many random binary trees, where each split randomly picks a feature and a split value; an anomalous point, being different from the bulk of the data, tends to get separated into its own leaf after very few splits, while a normal point buried in a dense region takes many splits to isolate. The anomaly score is derived from the average path length (number of splits) across all trees in the forest, normalized so scores near 1 mean likely anomaly and scores near 0 (or the sklearn convention of negative decision_function values) mean likely normal. Isolation Forest handles multivariate structure (unlike z-score/IQR) and scales well to high dimensions and large datasets since it doesn't need distance computations between all pairs of points. The key hyperparameter, contamination, is your estimate of what fraction of the data is anomalous — it only affects where the decision threshold is drawn, not the underlying scores. |
| **Worked example**      | from sklearn.ensemble import IsolationForest iso = IsolationForest(n_estimators=200, contamination=0.02, random_state=0) iso.fit(X) scores = iso.decision_function(X) \# higher = more normal preds = iso.predict(X) \# 1 = normal, -1 = anomaly print((preds == -1).sum(), 'flagged as anomalies out of', len(X))                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |

**Knowledge check:** Why does Isolation Forest need fewer splits, on average, to isolate an anomalous point than a normal one?

\(A\) Anomalous points are always labeled in the training data

**(B) Anomalies sit in sparse regions of feature space distinct from the bulk of normal points, so random partitioning separates them from everything else much faster**

\(C\) Isolation Forest always places anomalies at the root of every tree by design

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Fit an IsolationForest on a multivariate dataset with contamination=0.05, inspect the lowest decision_function scores, and compare those flagged points against what the univariate z-score/IQR methods from the previous lecture would have flagged on each feature individually.

**Lecture 273 anomaly detection**

*Year 2 · Month 16 · Unsupervised Learning · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
|-------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Use Local Outlier Factor (LOF) to find anomalies that are only unusual relative to their local neighborhood density.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
| **Teacher explanation** | Local Outlier Factor detects anomalies by comparing each point's local density to the local density of its neighbors, which lets it catch anomalies that a global method would miss: a point sitting in a sparse region can be perfectly normal if its whole neighborhood is sparse (e.g. a legitimately remote rural location), while a point in a dense cluster can be anomalous if it's noticeably less dense than its immediate surroundings (e.g. one data point slightly apart within an otherwise tight cluster). LOF computes, for each point, its 'local reachability density' based on distances to its k nearest neighbors, then compares that density to the average density of those same neighbors — an LOF score near 1 means similar density to neighbors (normal), while a score well above 1 means the point is in a notably sparser region than its neighbors (anomalous). This 'local' comparison is LOF's key advantage over Isolation Forest and distance-based methods, which implicitly assume one global notion of 'far' or 'close' across the whole dataset — LOF instead adapts to datasets where normal density varies by region (e.g. combining urban and rural geographic data, or combining low-traffic and high-traffic account types). |
| **Worked example**      | from sklearn.neighbors import LocalOutlierFactor lof = LocalOutlierFactor(n_neighbors=20, contamination=0.03) preds = lof.fit_predict(X) \# 1 = normal, -1 = anomaly scores = lof.negative_outlier_factor\_ \# more negative = more anomalous print((preds == -1).sum(), 'flagged by LOF') \# compare: LOF can flag a point Isolation Forest misses if it's only LOCALLY sparse                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |

**Knowledge check:** What makes LOF able to detect anomalies that a purely global method (like a single z-score threshold across the whole dataset) would miss?

\(A\) LOF requires labeled training data, which makes it inherently more accurate

**(B) LOF compares each point's density to its own local neighbors' density rather than to one fixed global density, so it adapts to regions of a dataset with naturally varying density**

\(C\) LOF only works on two-dimensional data

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Run LOF with n_neighbors=20 on a dataset that mixes a dense and a sparse region (e.g. simulate two clusters with very different spreads), and identify any points LOF flags that a simple global distance threshold would not have flagged.

**Lecture 274 anomaly detection**

*Year 2 · Month 16 · Unsupervised Learning · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               |
|-------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Build a fraud-detection anomaly pipeline, handle extreme class imbalance, and choose an operating threshold with precision/recall.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
| **Teacher explanation** | Credit card fraud detection is the textbook anomaly-detection business case because fraud is rare (often under 0.5% of transactions), making it a severe class-imbalance problem where plain accuracy is meaningless (predicting 'not fraud' for everything already gives 99.5% accuracy). The workflow: engineer features (transaction amount, time since last transaction, deviation from the account's typical spend, merchant category), fit both Isolation Forest and LOF on the (mostly legitimate) transaction data, and combine their anomaly scores — points both methods flag are higher-confidence fraud candidates than points only one flags. Because flagging every transaction for manual review is too costly and missing real fraud is also costly, you choose an operating threshold by looking at the precision-recall tradeoff directly (not ROC-AUC alone, which is misleadingly optimistic under heavy imbalance): higher thresholds give higher precision (fewer false alarms sent to the fraud team) but lower recall (more real fraud slips through), and the right point on that curve is a business decision, not a purely statistical one, driven by the cost of a missed fraud versus the cost of a false alarm. |
| **Worked example**      | from sklearn.ensemble import IsolationForest from sklearn.neighbors import LocalOutlierFactor from sklearn.metrics import precision_recall_curve iso_scores = IsolationForest(contamination=0.01, random_state=0).fit(X).decision_function(X) lof_scores = LocalOutlierFactor(n_neighbors=20, contamination=0.01).fit(X).negative_outlier_factor\_ combined = -iso_scores + -lof_scores \# higher combined = more suspicious precision, recall, thresholds = precision_recall_curve(y_true_fraud_labels, combined) \# pick threshold balancing cost of false alarms vs missed fraud                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |

**Knowledge check:** Why is plain classification accuracy a poor metric for a fraud-detection model when fraud is only 0.5% of transactions?

\(A\) Accuracy cannot be computed when labels are imbalanced

**(B) A model that always predicts 'not fraud' would score 99.5% accuracy while catching zero real fraud, so accuracy hides the model's actual usefulness**

\(C\) Accuracy only applies to regression problems, not classification

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** On a labeled fraud dataset (or a simulated imbalanced dataset), fit Isolation Forest and LOF, combine their scores, plot a precision-recall curve, and pick and justify one operating threshold.

**Lecture 275 anomaly detection**

*Year 2 · Month 16 · Unsupervised Learning · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
|-------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Evaluate anomaly detectors correctly with and without ground-truth labels, and avoid the common anomaly-detection mistakes.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               |
| **Teacher explanation** | Evaluating anomaly detection splits into two very different situations. When you have ground-truth labels (confirmed fraud, confirmed defects), you can compute real classification metrics — precision, recall, F1, precision@k (precision among the top-k most suspicious points, which matches how an analyst team actually works through a ranked queue), and ROC-AUC, though AUC should be read cautiously under heavy imbalance. When you have NO labels, the usual case for genuinely novel anomalies, you can't compute precision/recall at all; you instead rely on qualitative checks: do flagged points look different on manual inspection, does the flagged fraction roughly match your contamination assumption, and are results stable across re-runs or across a few algorithms (Isolation Forest, LOF, z-score) agreeing on the same points. The classic mistakes to guard against: setting contamination to an arbitrary round number instead of a domain-informed estimate, treating the same features' scale inconsistently across the univariate (z-score/IQR), tree-based (Isolation Forest), and density-based (LOF) methods, and assuming any one anomaly-detection algorithm is universally best — the right choice depends on whether anomalies are expected to be global outliers, locally sparse points, or isolable via random partitioning. |
| **Worked example**      | \# unlabeled case: check agreement across methods as a sanity check iso_flags = set(np.where(IsolationForest(contamination=0.02, random_state=0).fit_predict(X) == -1)\[0\]) lof_flags = set(np.where(LocalOutlierFactor(contamination=0.02).fit_predict(X) == -1)\[0\]) agreement = iso_flags & lof_flags print(len(agreement), 'points flagged by BOTH methods -- higher-confidence anomalies') \# labeled case: from sklearn.metrics import precision_score, recall_score, roc_auc_score                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               |

**Knowledge check:** When you have no ground-truth anomaly labels at all, what is a reasonable way to gain confidence in a set of flagged points?

\(A\) Compute ROC-AUC against the unknown labels

**(B) Check whether multiple different anomaly-detection methods (e.g. Isolation Forest and LOF) agree on flagging the same points, and whether the flagged fraction roughly matches domain expectations**

\(C\) Assume accuracy of exactly 95% by convention

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Run Isolation Forest, LOF, and the z-score/IQR methods from lecture 271 on the same unlabeled dataset, find the points all three flag, and write a short note on how confident you'd be recommending those specific points for manual review.

*Year 2 · Month 16 · Unsupervised Learning · 1 guided hour + homework*

There is no external certification tied to this month — the assessment is the program's own internal knowledge check, scored against the course's standard 80% internal passing bar, and is meant to confirm you can pick the right unsupervised technique for a described business scenario, not just recite definitions. |

**Month 17 Time Series**

**Lecture 277 Time-series structure**

*Year 2 · Month 17 · Time Series · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
|-------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Decompose a time series into trend, seasonal, and residual components and distinguish additive from multiplicative decomposition.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| **Teacher explanation** | Any time series can be thought of as a combination of trend (the long-run direction, up/down/flat), seasonality (a pattern that repeats at a fixed, known period — weekly, monthly, yearly), and residual/noise (whatever's left after removing trend and seasonality, ideally unpredictable). Decomposition is additive, series = trend + seasonal + residual, when the seasonal swing stays roughly constant in absolute size regardless of the trend's level; it's multiplicative, series = trend \* seasonal \* residual, when the seasonal swing grows proportionally as the trend level grows (common in sales data: a retailer's December spike is bigger in dollar terms once the business has grown). Choosing the wrong decomposition type is a real, visible mistake: forcing additive decomposition onto a series whose seasonal amplitude clearly grows with the trend will produce a residual component that still has visible seasonal-looking wiggle in it, meaning the decomposition didn't fully separate the signal. |
| **Worked example**      | from statsmodels.tsa.seasonal import seasonal_decompose import pandas as pd ts = pd.read_csv('monthly_sales.csv', index_col='date', parse_dates=True)\['sales'\] result = seasonal_decompose(ts, model='multiplicative', period=12) result.plot() \# shows trend, seasonal, resid panels print(result.resid.std()) \# smaller residual std = cleaner decomposition fit                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |

**Knowledge check:** A retail sales series shows a seasonal December spike that gets larger in absolute dollar terms every year as the business grows. Which decomposition model fits better?

\(A\) Additive, because the spike always happens in December

**(B) Multiplicative, because the seasonal effect scales with the trend's level rather than staying a fixed absolute amount**

\(C\) Neither model type applies to retail data

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Load a monthly time series with a visible trend, run seasonal_decompose with model='additive' and model='multiplicative', plot both, and identify which leaves a cleaner (less seasonal-looking) residual.

**Lecture 278 Time-series structure**

*Year 2 · Month 17 · Time Series · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
|-------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Test a series for stationarity with the Augmented Dickey-Fuller test and use differencing, ACF, and PACF to understand its autocorrelation structure.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
| **Teacher explanation** | A series is stationary if its statistical properties (mean, variance, autocorrelation) don't change over time — most forecasting models assume or require this. The Augmented Dickey-Fuller (ADF) test formally checks for a unit root (non-stationarity): the null hypothesis is 'the series is non-stationary', so a small p-value (conventionally below 0.05) lets you reject that null and conclude the series is likely stationary. A non-stationary series (one with a trend) is typically made stationary by differencing — subtracting each value from the previous one (first difference) removes a linear trend; if seasonality remains, a seasonal difference (subtracting the value from one full period ago) removes that too. The autocorrelation function (ACF) plots correlation between the series and its own lagged values at each lag, while the partial autocorrelation function (PACF) plots the correlation at each lag AFTER removing the effect of all shorter lags — together these two plots are the standard diagnostic for identifying how many autoregressive or moving-average terms a model like ARIMA should use. |
| **Worked example**      | from statsmodels.tsa.stattools import adfuller from statsmodels.graphics.tsaplots import plot_acf, plot_pacf result = adfuller(ts) print('ADF p-value:', result\[1\]) \# \> 0.05 suggests non-stationary ts_diff = ts.diff().dropna() print('After differencing, ADF p-value:', adfuller(ts_diff)\[1\]) plot_acf(ts_diff, lags=24); plot_pacf(ts_diff, lags=24)                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |

**Knowledge check:** An ADF test on a raw series returns a p-value of 0.63. What should you conclude and do next?

\(A\) The series is clearly stationary; proceed directly to modeling

**(B) The series is likely non-stationary (fail to reject the null); apply differencing and re-run the ADF test**

\(C\) The p-value means the series has no seasonality

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Run the ADF test on a raw time series, then on its first-differenced version, report both p-values, and plot the ACF/PACF of the differenced series.

**Lecture 279 Time-series structure**

*Year 2 · Month 17 · Time Series · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
|-------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Decompose a real-world dataset (e.g. monthly airline passengers or retail sales) and explain the business meaning of each extracted component.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| **Teacher explanation** | This worked example takes a genuinely messy real dataset — monthly airline passenger counts or monthly retail sales — and walks through the full decomposition-and-interpretation workflow a business analyst would actually do: load and resample the data to a consistent monthly frequency, visually inspect for an obvious trend and seasonal period (12 months is the default guess for monthly data, confirmed by a peak in the ACF at lag 12), run seasonal_decompose, and then translate each output panel into a sentence a non-technical stakeholder would understand — e.g. 'the underlying trend component shows 4% year-over-year growth after removing the seasonal summer travel spike, and the residual component shows an unusual dip in April 2020 that the trend/seasonal model doesn't explain' (a real anomaly worth flagging, connecting back to Month 16's anomaly detection). This is the step most students skip: decomposition alone is not the final deliverable, the business interpretation of it is. |
| **Worked example**      | import pandas as pd from statsmodels.tsa.seasonal import seasonal_decompose ts = pd.read_csv('airline_passengers.csv', index_col='Month', parse_dates=True)\['Passengers'\] result = seasonal_decompose(ts, model='multiplicative', period=12) \# business narrative: trend_growth = (result.trend.dropna().iloc\[-1\] / result.trend.dropna().iloc\[0\]) \*\* (12/len(result.trend.dropna())) - 1 print(f'approx annualized trend growth: {trend_growth:.1%}') biggest_residual_month = result.resid.abs().idxmax() print('largest unexplained deviation at:', biggest_residual_month)                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |

**Knowledge check:** After decomposing a sales series, the residual component shows one month with an unusually large deviation that trend and seasonality don't explain. What does that specific finding suggest doing next?

\(A\) Ignore it, since residuals are expected to be exactly zero

**(B) Investigate that specific month as a potential anomaly or one-off event (e.g. a promotion, supply disruption, or data error) worth flagging to the business**

\(C\) Immediately conclude the entire decomposition model is invalid

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Decompose a real monthly dataset (airline passengers or similar), identify the month with the largest residual, and write two sentences hypothesizing a business reason for that specific deviation.

**Lecture 280 Time-series structure**

*Year 2 · Month 17 · Time Series · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
|-------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Debug common time-series handling mistakes: broken date indices, incorrect resampling, and leakage from a non-time-respecting train/test split.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| **Teacher explanation** | Time-series data breaks in ways cross-sectional (tabular, non-temporal) data doesn't. Common mistakes: parsing dates inconsistently or leaving the index as plain strings/objects instead of a proper pandas DatetimeIndex, which silently breaks .resample() and plotting order; resampling at the wrong frequency or aggregation (e.g. using .sum() when the right aggregation for a stock price is .last() or .mean(), not sum); leaving gaps in the date index (a missing week looks identical to a week of zero sales unless you explicitly reindex and check for NaNs); and — the most damaging mistake — splitting train/test randomly (as you would for i.i.d. tabular data) instead of by time, which leaks future information into the training set and makes a forecasting model look far more accurate during evaluation than it will be in production, since a random split lets the model 'see' data points that occur chronologically after the test points it's being evaluated on. |
| **Worked example**      | import pandas as pd df\['date'\] = pd.to_datetime(df\['date'\]) \# ensure real datetime, not string df = df.set_index('date').sort_index() full_range = pd.date_range(df.index.min(), df.index.max(), freq='D') df = df.reindex(full_range) \# exposes any missing dates as NaN rows print(df.isna().sum()) \# CORRECT time-respecting split: cutoff = '2024-01-01' train, test = df\[:cutoff\], df\[cutoff:\] \# NOT train_test_split(..., shuffle=True)                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |

**Knowledge check:** Why is a random (shuffled) train/test split inappropriate for evaluating a time-series forecasting model?

\(A\) Random splits are always faster to compute, so this is purely a performance concern

**(B) A random split lets the model train on data points that occur chronologically after some test points, leaking future information and making evaluation unrealistically optimistic**

\(C\) Random splits only work for classification problems, not regression

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Take a date-indexed series, reindex it to a complete daily range to expose any missing dates, then create a correct time-respecting train/test split using a cutoff date rather than sklearn's shuffled train_test_split.

**Lecture 281 baselines**

*Year 2 · Month 17 · Time Series · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
|-------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Build a naive forecast and a naive seasonal forecast, and explain why every serious forecasting project must start with one.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
