**Homework:** Train the same network with dropout left 'on' at test time (by calling the model in training mode during evaluation) and compare predictions across repeated calls on the same single input — you should see the predictions vary randomly, demonstrating concretely why dropout must be disabled at inference.

**Lecture 447 regularization**

*Year 3 · Month 26 · Deep Learning · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
|-------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Combine early stopping with weight decay and dropout into a complete regularization strategy, tying this topic's pieces together on the overfitting dataset used across this run of lectures.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
| **Teacher explanation** | Early stopping is the simplest and often most effective regularization technique: monitor validation loss during training and stop (keeping the best-seen weights) once it fails to improve for a set number of epochs (the 'patience'), which directly targets the overfitting signature diagnosed in lecture 443 — rather than trying to prevent overfitting from happening at all, early stopping simply stops training at the point just before the training/validation gap starts widening. In Keras, \`tf.keras.callbacks.EarlyStopping(monitor='val_loss', patience=5, restore_best_weights=True)\` passed to \`model.fit()\` implements this automatically, and combining it with L2 weight decay and dropout from the previous two lectures gives a complete, standard regularization toolkit: weight decay constrains weight magnitudes throughout training, dropout prevents over-reliance on specific neuron combinations, and early stopping provides a final safety net that catches whatever overfitting the other two didn't fully prevent. On the same dataset used across this three-lecture arc, applying all three together typically closes the train/validation gap dramatically more than any single technique alone, which is the empirical lesson this synthesis lecture is built to demonstrate directly, side by side, on one chart showing four curves (unregularized baseline, L2 only, L2+dropout, and L2+dropout+early-stopping). The broader principle for students heading into later months (CNNs, transformers) is that these three techniques — weight decay, dropout, early stopping — are not specific to feedforward networks; they reappear, sometimes under different names, across essentially every deep learning architecture covered later in the program. |
| **Worked example**      | Build and train four versions of the same network on the same dataset: (1) no regularization, (2) L2 weight decay only, (3) L2 + dropout, (4) L2 + dropout + EarlyStopping(patience=5) — plot all four (train_loss, val_loss) pairs on one figure and report, in a one-paragraph summary, the final validation loss and the epoch at which each version effectively stopped improving.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |

**Knowledge check:** What specific overfitting-related risk does early stopping address that weight decay and dropout do not directly solve on their own?

**(A) Even with weight decay and dropout applied, some residual overfitting can still occur the longer training continues; early stopping halts training at the point just before the validation loss starts to worsen, regardless of how much intrinsic regularization is already in the model**

\(B\) Early stopping is mathematically redundant with weight decay and produces exactly identical results, so combining them has no additional effect

\(C\) Early stopping is the only one of the three techniques that can be applied to a convolutional network; the other two only work on dense layers

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Complete the four-version comparison from the example and write a one-paragraph recommendation for which combination you would deploy, citing the specific validation loss numbers you observed as justification.

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |

Students should be able to explain, cold, why ReLU avoids the saturation problem that makes deep sigmoid networks hard to train, why backpropagation reuses layer-by-layer gradients rather than recomputing from scratch, and what a widening train/validation loss gap specifically indicates and which three techniques close it. |

**(A) The model has begun overfitting after roughly epoch 10, and techniques like weight decay, dropout, or early stopping around that epoch would directly address it**

\(B\) The model is underfitting throughout training because training loss never reaches exactly zero

**Lecture 449 Text preprocessing**

*Year 3 · Month 27 · NLP · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
|-------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Explain and implement tokenization mechanics — splitting raw text into words and sentences — as the foundational first step of any NLP pipeline.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
| **Teacher explanation** | Tokenization is the process of splitting raw text into discrete units (tokens): word tokenization splits on whitespace and punctuation boundaries, while sentence tokenization splits on sentence-ending punctuation, but both are genuinely harder than they first appear because of edge cases — 'Dr. Smith went to the U.S.' contains three periods, only one of which actually ends a sentence, and naive whitespace splitting on "don't" or "state-of-the-art" produces different, debatable token boundaries depending on the application. NLTK's \`word_tokenize\` and \`sent_tokenize\` use a trained, rule-based model (Punkt) that handles many of these abbreviation and punctuation edge cases correctly out of the box, while spaCy's tokenizer uses a combination of rules and exception lists tuned per-language and is generally faster and more production-oriented; both differ meaningfully from a naive \`.split()\` on whitespace, which is why a real pipeline should use a proper tokenizer rather than hand-rolled string splitting. The choice of tokenizer genuinely changes downstream results: a model trained on NLTK-tokenized text and evaluated on spaCy-tokenized text (or vice versa) can see a measurable, avoidable performance drop purely from token-boundary mismatches, which is why consistency of tokenizer choice across training and inference is a real production concern, not a pedantic detail. |
| **Worked example**      | \`\`\`python import nltk nltk.download('punkt') text = "Dr. Smith said the U.S. economy grew. It's the best quarter yet." print(nltk.sent_tokenize(text)) \# correctly finds 2 sentences, not 4 print(nltk.word_tokenize(text)) \# 'It's' -\> \['It', "'s"\], not one token \`\`\` Compare this to \`text.split()\`, which incorrectly treats 'U.S.' and the following word as one broken token and cannot find sentence boundaries at all.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |

**Knowledge check:** Why does naive whitespace splitting (\`text.split()\`) fail to correctly tokenize a sentence containing 'U.S.' or "don't"?

**(A) Whitespace splitting has no model of punctuation context, so it cannot distinguish a period that ends a sentence from one that is part of an abbreviation, or correctly separate a contraction into its two meaningful parts**

\(B\) Whitespace splitting only works on text written in languages other than English

\(C\) Python's split() function has a hard limit of one split per sentence and cannot process abbreviations at all

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Take a paragraph of real text containing at least two abbreviations and one contraction, tokenize it with both naive .split() and nltk.word_tokenize(), and list every case where the two approaches disagree.

**Lecture 450 Text preprocessing**

*Year 3 · Month 27 · NLP · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
|-------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Explain and apply stemming and lemmatization, understanding the mechanical difference between crude suffix-stripping and dictionary-aware word normalization.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |
| **Teacher explanation** | Stemming and lemmatization both aim to reduce a word to a common base form so that 'running', 'runs', and 'ran' are treated as related for downstream tasks like search or classification, but they do this very differently. Stemming (e.g., NLTK's Porter or Snowball stemmer) applies a fixed set of mechanical suffix-stripping rules with no understanding of the word's actual meaning or part of speech — it is fast but crude, and it can produce a result that is not even a real word, for example 'studies' stems to 'studi' under Porter, and unrelated words can accidentally collapse to the same stem (overstemming) while related words can fail to collapse (understemming, e.g. 'ran' does not stem to the same root as 'run' because stemming doesn't know they're the same verb). Lemmatization (e.g., spaCy's or NLTK's WordNet lemmatizer) instead maps a word to its dictionary base form (the 'lemma') using either a lookup dictionary or a part-of-speech-aware model, so 'ran' correctly lemmatizes to 'run' and 'studies' lemmatizes to the proper word 'study' — but lemmatization is slower and, crucially, needs to know the word's part of speech to be accurate, since 'leaves' lemmatizes to 'leaf' as a noun but to 'leave' as a verb. The practical choice: stemming suits quick, large-scale information-retrieval tasks (search engines) where speed matters more than perfect accuracy, while lemmatization suits tasks where the exact, readable base form matters, such as downstream text generation or careful feature engineering for a classifier. |
| **Worked example**      | \`\`\`python from nltk.stem import PorterStemmer from nltk.stem import WordNetLemmatizer stemmer, lemmatizer = PorterStemmer(), WordNetLemmatizer() words = \['running', 'studies', 'ran', 'leaves'\] print(\[stemmer.stem(w) for w in words\]) \# \['run', 'studi', 'ran', 'leav'\] print(\[lemmatizer.lemmatize(w, pos='v') for w in words\]) \# \['run', 'study', 'run', 'leave'\] \`\`\` Note 'ran' only correctly reduces to 'run' with the lemmatizer, and 'studi' from stemming is not a real English word.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |

**Knowledge check:** Why does the Porter stemmer reduce 'studies' to 'studi' instead of the real word 'study'?

**(A) Stemming applies mechanical suffix-stripping rules with no dictionary or linguistic knowledge, so it can produce a truncated string that isn't an actual word, as long as the rule matched**

\(B\) 'studi' is a deliberate placeholder NLTK uses internally that gets automatically corrected before any downstream task sees it

\(C\) Stemming always produces identical output to lemmatization for every word except irregular verbs

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Pick 10 words including at least 2 irregular verbs (like 'ran', 'went') and compare stemmer vs. lemmatizer output for each, noting every case where stemming produces a non-word or fails to normalize an irregular form correctly.

**Lecture 451 Text preprocessing**

*Year 3 · Month 27 · NLP · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
|-------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Apply stop-word removal, n-gram extraction, and text normalization (casing and punctuation handling), understanding when each helps and when it discards useful signal.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
| **Teacher explanation** | Stop-word removal strips extremely common words ('the', 'is', 'and', 'a') that carry little discriminative meaning for many tasks, reducing feature-space size and noise for classical bag-of-words models — but it is not universally beneficial: for tasks sensitive to syntax or sentiment nuance (e.g., 'not good' vs. 'good'), removing 'not' as a stop word can flip the actual meaning of a phrase, which is why sentiment-analysis pipelines often use a custom, shorter stop-word list that explicitly excludes negation words. N-grams extend single-word (unigram) tokens to contiguous sequences of N words — bigrams capture two-word phrases ('New York', 'not good'), trigrams capture three-word sequences — and including bigrams/trigrams alongside unigrams in a bag-of-words or TF-IDF representation lets a classical model capture some local word-order information it would otherwise completely lose, at the cost of a much larger, sparser feature space. Text normalization covers lowercasing (reduces 'The' and 'the' to the same token, usually beneficial, though it discards a signal like proper-noun capitalization that some tasks genuinely need), punctuation removal or standardization, and handling of numbers/currency/dates (sometimes replaced with placeholder tokens like \`\<NUM\>\` so the model generalizes across specific values rather than treating '42' and '43' as entirely unrelated tokens) — each of these choices is a genuine design decision with task-specific trade-offs, not a mechanical default to apply blindly. |
| **Worked example**      | \`\`\`python from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import CountVectorizer text = \['this movie is not good', 'this movie is good'\] vec_uni = CountVectorizer(ngram_range=(1,1), stop_words='english') print(vec_uni.fit_transform(text).toarray(), vec_uni.get_feature_names_out()) \# 'not' removed as a stop word -\> both sentences look nearly identical, losing the negation! vec_bi = CountVectorizer(ngram_range=(1,2)) \# no stop-word removal, unigrams+bigrams print(vec_bi.fit_transform(text).toarray(), vec_bi.get_feature_names_out()) \# 'not good' survives as its own bigram feature, preserving the negation signal \`\`\`                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |

**Knowledge check:** Why can removing stop words actually hurt a sentiment-analysis task, even though it generally helps reduce noise for other text classification tasks?

**(A) Common negation words like 'not' are often included in default stop-word lists, and removing them can make 'not good' look nearly identical to 'good' in the resulting feature representation**

\(B\) Stop-word removal always improves every NLP task uniformly and has no documented downside in any scenario

\(C\) Stop-word lists are language-specific and simply do not exist for the English language, making this a non-issue

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Using the CountVectorizer example, build a small custom stop-word list that excludes 'not', 'no', and 'never', and show that it preserves the negation signal that the default English stop-word list destroys.

**Lecture 452 Text preprocessing**

*Year 3 · Month 27 · NLP · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               |
|-------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Build a complete preprocessing pipeline for a real noisy text corpus (tweets), handling the specific artifacts of social-media text that clean, formal text does not have.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
| **Teacher explanation** | Social-media text (tweets, reviews, forum posts) has preprocessing challenges that clean, formal text (news articles, books) largely avoids: hashtags (\`#MondayMotivation\`) and @-mentions (\`@username\`) need an explicit decision — strip them, extract the text inside a hashtag as a regular word, or keep them as distinct features depending on whether the task cares about social context; URLs and emoji need to be either removed or replaced with placeholder tokens (\`\<URL\>\`), since raw URLs are nearly always noise for a classifier but their presence or absence can itself be a useful binary feature; and informal spelling (repeated letters for emphasis like 'sooo good', abbreviations like 'u' for 'you', inconsistent capitalization used for emphasis like ALL-CAPS) requires either a normalization dictionary or acceptance that some signal will simply be noisy. A realistic sentiment-analysis preprocessing pipeline for tweets, in order, typically: lowercases text, replaces URLs and @-mentions with placeholder tokens, extracts hashtag text as regular words (stripping the '#'), collapses repeated characters (regex \`r'(.)\1{2,}'\` down to 2 repeats, so 'sooo' becomes 'soo' rather than being treated as an entirely novel, unseen token), tokenizes, optionally removes a negation-aware stop-word list (per the previous lecture), and lemmatizes. Each step in this pipeline is a genuine, debatable design choice with a different right answer depending on the exact downstream task — there is no single 'correct' preprocessing pipeline, only one that is well-justified for your specific goal. |
| **Worked example**      | \`\`\`python import re def preprocess_tweet(text): text = text.lower() text = re.sub(r'http\S+', '\<URL\>', text) text = re.sub(r'@\w+', '\<USER\>', text) text = re.sub(r'#(\w+)', r'\1', text) \# strip '#' but keep the word text = re.sub(r'(.)\1{2,}', r'\1\1', text) \# 'sooooo' -\> 'soo' return text print(preprocess_tweet('@nasa this is sooooo cool!! check it out \#MondayMotivation http://t.co/xyz')) \`\`\`                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |

**Knowledge check:** In the tweet-preprocessing pipeline, why is a repeated-character collapse (\`r'(.)\1{2,}'\`) applied before tokenization rather than left untouched?

**(A) Without it, emphasis spellings like 'sooooo', 'soooo', and 'sooo' would each be treated as a completely distinct, unseen token, fragmenting the vocabulary and losing the shared meaning across all these variants**

\(B\) The regex is required by Python's re module and will throw a SyntaxError if omitted from any text-cleaning function

\(C\) Collapsing repeated characters is only relevant for languages other than English and has no effect on English-language social media text

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Collect 10 real tweets (or write 10 tweet-style sentences) containing at least one hashtag, one mention, one URL, and one emphasis-spelling each, run them through the preprocess_tweet function, and report what each transformation changed.

**Lecture 453 Text preprocessing**

*Year 3 · Month 27 · NLP · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
|-------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Apply regex-based text cleaning deliberately and diagnose the common mistake of over-cleaning text in a way that destroys information the downstream task actually needs.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
| **Teacher explanation** | Regex (regular expressions) is the primary tool for custom text cleaning beyond what a tokenizer or stemmer handles automatically — stripping HTML tags (\`re.sub(r'\<\[^\>\]+\>', '', text)\`), standardizing whitespace (\`re.sub(r'\s+', ' ', text)\`), or removing specific unwanted characters — but regex-based cleaning is a sharp tool that is easy to overuse. The most common over-cleaning mistake is blanket punctuation removal (\`re.sub(r'\[^\w\s\]', '', text)\`) applied without exception to a task where punctuation genuinely carries signal: stripping all punctuation from a sarcasm- or emotion-detection task destroys exclamation marks and question marks that are themselves meaningful features, and stripping it from a code-mixed or technical corpus can merge genuinely distinct tokens ('C++' becomes 'C', losing the language name entirely). A second common mistake is overly aggressive number handling — replacing every digit with a placeholder can be correct for a general sentiment classifier (where '42' vs '43' usually doesn't matter) but is actively harmful for a financial-document or medical-text classifier where the specific number (a dosage, a dollar amount) is exactly the information the model needs to extract. The general debugging principle, consistent with every other lecture in this program: before applying any cleaning step broadly, inspect a sample of cleaned output next to the original to confirm the step is removing noise and not removing signal specific to your task — a quick diff-style comparison on 10-20 real examples catches most over-cleaning mistakes before they propagate through an entire pipeline. |
| **Worked example**      | Take 5 real product reviews containing exclamation marks and a numeric rating mentioned in the text (e.g., 'I'd give this 9 out of 10!!'). Apply blanket punctuation+number stripping and show the result loses both the enthusiasm signal (the exclamation marks) and the actual rating (the numbers) — then write a more careful cleaning function that preserves \`!\`, \`?\`, and digits while still removing HTML tags and extra whitespace, and compare outputs side by side.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |

**Knowledge check:** Why can blanket punctuation removal hurt a sarcasm- or sentiment-detection classifier specifically, even though it is often harmless for a topic-classification task?

**(A) Punctuation like exclamation marks and question marks often carries genuine emotional or tonal signal that sentiment/sarcasm detection depends on, while topic classification cares more about the presence of specific content words**

\(B\) Punctuation removal is technically impossible to implement correctly in Python regardless of the task, which is why it should never be attempted

\(C\) Sarcasm detection models are incapable of processing any text that has been cleaned with regular expressions, by design

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Using the 5 reviews from the example, build and compare a 'blanket cleaning' function and a 'task-aware cleaning' function that explicitly preserves punctuation relevant to sentiment, and write two sentences on which one you'd choose for a sentiment classifier and why.

**Lecture 454 Text preprocessing**

*Year 3 · Month 27 · NLP · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
|-------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Explain part-of-speech tagging and named entity recognition as structured preprocessing steps that extract grammatical and semantic information beyond simple token cleaning.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| **Teacher explanation** | Part-of-speech (POS) tagging assigns each token a grammatical category (noun, verb, adjective, etc.) using a model trained on large tagged corpora — spaCy's \`token.pos\_\` gives this directly, and it is exactly the information lemmatization needs to correctly disambiguate words like 'leaves' (noun vs. verb) from the earlier lecture, making POS tagging a genuine preprocessing dependency, not just a downstream analysis output. Named entity recognition (NER) identifies spans of text referring to real-world entities — person names, organizations, locations, dates, monetary amounts — and tags each span with its entity type; spaCy's pretrained English model, via \`doc.ents\`, can pull 'Apple' as an ORG, 'Tim Cook' as a PERSON, and '\$3 billion' as MONEY directly out of raw text, which is enormously useful both as a preprocessing step (replacing specific entity text with a generic placeholder like \`\<PERSON\>\` so a classifier generalizes across different names) and as a standalone feature-extraction task (building a structured database of companies and amounts mentioned across a corpus of news articles). Both POS tagging and NER are themselves machine-learned models (today, usually transformer-based under the hood, though spaCy's smaller models use more classical statistical sequence tagging), and their accuracy depends heavily on domain match — a model trained on news text will mis-tag medical or legal jargon, which is a genuine limitation to check before trusting NER output on a specialized corpus without domain-specific fine-tuning or validation. |
| **Worked example**      | \`\`\`python import spacy nlp = spacy.load('en_core_web_sm') doc = nlp("Apple's CEO Tim Cook announced \$3 billion in new investment in Austin.") for token in doc: print(token.text, token.pos\_) for ent in doc.ents: print(ent.text, ent.label\_) \# Apple ORG, Tim Cook PERSON, \$3 billion MONEY, Austin GPE \`\`\`                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |

**Knowledge check:** Why is a named-entity-recognition model trained on general news text likely to perform worse when applied directly to medical clinical notes without any adaptation?

**(A) NER models learn entity patterns from the specific vocabulary and context of their training domain, so unfamiliar medical terminology and entity types (drug names, dosages) fall outside what the model learned to recognize reliably**

\(B\) NER models can only process text that contains at least one company name, so medical text without company names will always fail to run

\(C\) spaCy's NER models are hard-coded to reject any text longer than a single sentence, regardless of domain

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Run spaCy's en_core_web_sm NER on 3 sentences from a specialized domain you know (medical, legal, or technical), and list every entity it correctly identified and every one it missed or mislabeled.

**Lecture 455 Text preprocessing**

*Year 3 · Month 27 · NLP · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
|-------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Synthesize tokenization, normalization, stop-word/n-gram decisions, regex cleaning, and POS/NER into one complete, justified preprocessing pipeline ready to feed a vectorization step.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
| **Teacher explanation** | This synthesis lecture assembles the full preprocessing arc into a single, ordered, production-shaped pipeline, making explicit the order dependencies that matter: text should generally be cleaned (HTML/URL/regex-based noise removal from lecture 453) before tokenization, because cleaning raw-text artifacts first prevents a tokenizer from producing broken tokens out of HTML tags or URLs; tokenization happens before stemming/lemmatization, which need individual tokens (and ideally POS tags, from lecture 454) to operate on; stop-word removal and n-gram extraction happen at or after tokenization and should be the last decisions made, since they are the most task-specific and most reversible if you decide to re-tune them. A complete, documented pipeline function should take raw text in and a vectorization-ready list of tokens out, with every design decision (which stop words were excluded and why, whether stemming or lemmatization was chosen and why, whether n-grams were included) stated explicitly as a comment or docstring, both so a future collaborator understands the choices and so you can systematically ablate (try removing) each step to measure its actual effect on downstream model performance — exactly the controlled-comparison discipline from Month 25's model-selection lectures, now applied to preprocessing choices rather than hyperparameters. This pipeline becomes the direct input to the vectorization and embedding lectures that follow this week, where you'll see concretely how different preprocessing choices change the resulting feature representations. |
| **Worked example**      | Write one function \`preprocess_pipeline(text, use_stemming=False, remove_stopwords=True, ngram_range=(1,1))\` that runs clean -\> tokenize -\> (stem or lemmatize) -\> (optionally remove stop words, preserving negation words) -\> return ready tokens, with clear docstring comments justifying each default. Run it on the same 5 product reviews from lecture 453 with three different parameter combinations and compare the resulting token lists.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |

**Knowledge check:** In the assembled preprocessing pipeline, why must regex-based cleaning (removing HTML tags, URLs) happen before tokenization rather than after?

**(A) Running a tokenizer on uncleaned text can split HTML tags or URLs into multiple broken, meaningless tokens, so cleaning first prevents that fragmentation from ever occurring**

\(B\) Tokenizers in Python physically cannot execute if any HTML or URL text is present anywhere in the input string

\(C\) The order makes no actual difference to the final token list; it is purely a stylistic convention with no functional impact

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Build the preprocess_pipeline function described in the example, run it with stemming and with lemmatization on the same input, and write two sentences on which produced more readable, interpretable tokens and why that might matter for a task where you need to explain model features to a stakeholder.

**Lecture 456 embeddings concepts**

*Year 3 · Month 27 · NLP · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
|-------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Explain one-hot encoding, bag-of-words, and TF-IDF mechanics as the classical, frequency-based route to turning text into numeric features.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
| **Teacher explanation** | One-hot encoding represents each word as a vector with a single 1 at that word's index in the vocabulary and 0 elsewhere — simple, but it produces enormous, extremely sparse vectors (one dimension per vocabulary word, easily tens of thousands) and, crucially, treats every word as equally unrelated to every other word, since the vectors for 'cat' and 'dog' are exactly as dissimilar (cosine similarity of 0) as 'cat' and 'bicycle'.
