**(A) Embedding vectors place semantically similar words close together in vector space, so a synonym unseen in training can still produce a feature vector close to what the model learned from related training words, whereas TF-IDF treats each vocabulary word as an entirely separate, unrelated dimension**

\(B\) TF-IDF classifiers are incapable of making any prediction on a document containing even a single word absent from the training vocabulary

\(C\) Embedding-based classifiers always require at least 10,000 training examples to function at all, while TF-IDF classifiers work with any amount of data

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Build the embedding-based classifier from the example and the TF-IDF+LogisticRegression classifier from two lectures ago on the same small training set, then test both on a held-out example that deliberately uses synonyms not present in training, comparing which one classifies it correctly.

**Lecture 465 text classification**

*Year 3 · Month 27 · NLP · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
|-------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Walk through a complete, realistic text classification project end to end — spam/sentiment detection on a real dataset — covering data loading, preprocessing, feature extraction, model training, and evaluation as one coherent pipeline.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
| **Teacher explanation** | This lecture assembles every preceding piece of this month's NLP arc into one realistic, complete project: load a real labeled dataset (e.g., the classic SMS Spam Collection or an IMDB movie review sentiment dataset), apply the full preprocessing pipeline from lecture 455 (clean, tokenize, lemmatize, handle stop words with negation preserved), extract TF-IDF features (or averaged embeddings, as an explicit comparison point), split into train/validation/test using the proper non-leaking procedure from Month 25, train several candidate models (Naive Bayes, logistic regression, LinearSVC) with cross-validation for model selection, and evaluate the final chosen model's precision, recall, F1, and confusion matrix on the held-out test set. This full-pipeline view makes explicit how much of the actual work in a real NLP project is preprocessing and feature-engineering decisions rather than model fitting — the model-training line of code is often one line, while the decisions about tokenization, stop words, and vectorization genuinely determine the ceiling on achievable performance, which is why this month built those pieces up carefully before this integration lecture rather than starting here. The evaluation should explicitly connect back to Month 25's lesson on metric choice under class imbalance: a spam dataset is often imbalanced (far more ham than spam), so precision/recall/F1 and a confusion matrix, not raw accuracy, are the metrics that should drive the final model choice and any discussion of the model's real-world readiness. |
| **Worked example**      | Load the SMS Spam Collection dataset (5,572 messages, ~13% spam), run it through \`preprocess_pipeline\` from lecture 455, vectorize with TF-IDF, cross-validate Naive Bayes vs. LogisticRegression vs. LinearSVC with \`StratifiedKFold(5)\` scoring on F1, select the winner, then report its confusion matrix and precision/recall on a held-out test split that was never touched during model selection.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |

**Knowledge check:** In a real spam-detection project with roughly 13% spam and 87% ham, why should the final model be chosen based on cross-validated F1 or recall rather than raw accuracy?

**(A) With most messages being ham, a model that simply predicts 'ham' for everything would already score around 87% accuracy while catching zero spam, so accuracy alone cannot distinguish a genuinely useful spam filter from a useless one**

\(B\) F1 score is mathematically identical to accuracy whenever the dataset contains text data, so the choice makes no practical difference

\(C\) Accuracy cannot be computed at all for text classification tasks, regardless of class balance, due to a limitation of scikit-learn's metrics module

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Complete the full spam-detection pipeline described in the example end to end, and write a one-paragraph summary (as if reporting to a stakeholder) stating the final model choice, its precision/recall trade-off, and whether you'd deploy it as-is or recommend further tuning.

**Lecture 466 text classification**

*Year 3 · Month 27 · NLP · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
|-------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Diagnose and fix common text-classification mistakes: class imbalance in text corpora, mismatched evaluation metrics, and overfitting on small corpora with too-large a vocabulary.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| **Teacher explanation** | This hands-on debugging lecture works through the mistakes students most often hit after lecture 465's full pipeline. Class imbalance in text data is pervasive (spam detection, fraud-complaint detection, rare-disease-mention extraction all skew heavily toward the majority class), and the Month 25 fixes apply directly here: stratified cross-validation, precision/recall/F1 or average-precision as the scoring metric instead of accuracy, and resampling techniques (SMOTE does not directly apply to sparse high-dimensional text features well, so class-weighting via \`class_weight='balanced'\` in LogisticRegression/LinearSVC, or simple random oversampling of minority-class documents, are the more common text-specific fixes). Mismatched evaluation metrics is a related but distinct mistake: optimizing a model's hyperparameters for accuracy when the actual business cost is asymmetric (missing a real spam message is a minor annoyance; flagging a legitimate business email as spam might cause a missed opportunity) means the model should be tuned and thresholded for the metric that reflects that asymmetry — adjusting the classification threshold away from the default 0.5 using the model's predicted probabilities, plotted via a precision-recall curve, directly controls this trade-off. Overfitting on small text corpora with too large a vocabulary is a specific, common text problem: TF-IDF with no \`max_features\` limit on a corpus of only a few hundred documents can produce more feature dimensions than training examples, which invites severe overfitting — setting \`max_features\` to a few thousand, requiring a minimum document frequency (\`min_df=2\`, dropping words that appear in only one document), or using dimensionality reduction (TruncatedSVD on the TF-IDF matrix, i.e. a lightweight form of topic modeling) are the standard, effective fixes. |
| **Worked example**      | On a small text dataset (under 500 documents), build a TF-IDF+LogisticRegression pipeline with no max_features limit and observe severe train/test accuracy gap (the overfitting signature from Month 26). Then rebuild with \`TfidfVectorizer(max_features=2000, min_df=2)\` and \`class_weight='balanced'\` on the LogisticRegression, and show both the reduced overfitting gap and improved minority-class recall.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               |

**Knowledge check:** Why can an unrestricted TF-IDF vectorizer on a small text corpus (a few hundred documents) lead to severe overfitting?

**(A) Without a max_features or min_df limit, the resulting feature-vector dimensionality can exceed the number of training documents, giving the model far more parameters than data points to constrain them**

\(B\) TF-IDF vectorizers always produce exactly 10,000 features regardless of corpus size, which is inherently too many for any dataset

\(C\) Overfitting in text classification is caused exclusively by the choice of model algorithm, never by the feature extraction step

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Reproduce the overfitting experiment from the example on your own small text dataset, report the train/test accuracy gap before and after applying max_features, min_df, and class_weight='balanced', and state which fix had the largest measurable effect.

| **Teacher explanation** | This closing lecture of the text-classification arc (and the month's final content lecture before the examination) brings every classifier type from this run together on one shared dataset and evaluation protocol: Naive Bayes as the fast, low-data-requirement generative baseline; TF-IDF plus logistic regression or LinearSVC as the strong, interpretable discriminative baseline most real projects should try first; and averaged-embedding features feeding a small neural classifier as the semantically-aware alternative that may generalize better to novel vocabulary at the cost of interpretability and training complexity. Following the exact statistical-comparison discipline from Month 25 (paired cross-validation scores, not just comparing mean numbers by eye), the mini-project should cross-validate all three approaches on the same folds, run a paired significance test between the top two contenders, and only then make a final recommendation that explicitly weighs the statistically-supported performance difference against practical deployment factors: Naive Bayes and linear models train and predict near-instantly and are trivial to deploy and explain; the embedding-based neural classifier needs a pretrained embedding file shipped with the application and a (small but nonzero) inference-time compute cost. The deliverable is a short written recommendation, exactly the kind of artifact a working data scientist produces at the end of a real text-classification project: which model, why (citing the cross-validated metric and the significance test result), and what the production trade-offs are. |
| **Worked example**      | Run Naive Bayes, TF-IDF+LinearSVC, and the averaged-embedding neural classifier with the same StratifiedKFold(5) splits on your spam or sentiment dataset from lecture 465, compute a paired t-test between the two best-performing models' per-fold F1 scores, and write a half-page recommendation memo stating your final model choice, citing the statistical result and at least one deployment consideration (inference speed, interpretability, or dependency size).                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |

**Knowledge check:** In this final comparison, why is a paired statistical test between the top two models' per-fold scores more rigorous than simply picking whichever model has the higher mean cross-validation score?

**(A) A paired test accounts for whether the observed mean difference is larger than what could plausibly arise from fold-to-fold variation alone, rather than treating any numeric difference in means as automatically meaningful**

\(B\) Paired tests are only used when comparing exactly three models simultaneously and cannot be applied to a two-model comparison

\(C\) The mean cross-validation score is mathematically undefined for text classifiers, making a statistical test the only valid comparison method

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Complete the three-model paired comparison and recommendation memo described in the example, explicitly stating the p-value you obtained and how it did or did not change your final recommendation versus just looking at the raw mean scores.

**Lecture 469 Images/tensors**

*Year 3 · Month 28 · Computer Vision · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
|-------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Explain how a digital image is represented as a multi-dimensional tensor and read its shape and dtype correctly.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| **Teacher explanation** | A digital image is a grid of pixels, and once loaded into a deep learning framework it becomes a tensor with shape (height, width, channels) for a single RGB image in NumPy/PIL convention, or (channels, height, width) in PyTorch's default convention. Each pixel value is an intensity, typically stored as an 8-bit unsigned integer (0-255) on disk but converted to float32 in \[0,1\] or standardized before feeding a network. A grayscale image has a single channel, while RGB has three (red, green, blue) and RGBA has four with an alpha transparency channel. Understanding this shape convention matters immediately: NumPy and PIL default to (H, W, C) channel-last ordering, while PyTorch tensors expect (C, H, W) channel-first, and mixing the two silently produces garbled images or shape-mismatch errors deep in a model. |
| **Worked example**      | Load a JPEG with PIL: img = Image.open('cat.jpg'), convert to a NumPy array arr = np.array(img) and print arr.shape (e.g. (375, 500, 3)) and arr.dtype (uint8). Convert to a PyTorch tensor with torch.from_numpy(arr).permute(2,0,1) to get shape (3, 375, 500), then scale to float with .float() / 255.0 and print the new dtype.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |

**Knowledge check:** A loaded RGB image array has shape (480, 640, 3) in NumPy/PIL convention. What does the final '3' represent?

**(A) The number of color channels (red, green, blue)**

\(B\) The batch size of 3 images stacked together

\(C\) The bit depth of each pixel (3 bits per channel)

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Load one of your own photos with PIL and NumPy, print its shape and dtype, then convert it to a PyTorch channel-first float tensor scaled to \[0,1\], printing the new shape and dtype at each step.

**Lecture 470 Images/tensors**

*Year 3 · Month 28 · Computer Vision · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
|-------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Convert between color spaces, resize images with different interpolation methods, and assemble a batch tensor of several images.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
| **Teacher explanation** | Beyond RGB, images are often converted to other color spaces: grayscale collapses channels using a weighted luminance formula (roughly 0.299R + 0.587G + 0.114B), while HSV (hue, saturation, value) separates color information from brightness and is useful for color-based filtering or augmentation. Resizing an image requires interpolation: nearest-neighbor is fast but blocky, bilinear smooths by averaging the four nearest pixels, and bicubic uses a wider neighborhood for sharper results, and the choice affects both visual quality and downstream model accuracy if training and inference use different methods. When many images are processed together they are stacked into a batch tensor of shape (N, C, H, W), which requires every image in the batch to share the same H and W, forcing a consistent resize or crop policy before batching. Memory layout matters at scale too: a batch of 64 images at 224x224x3 in float32 occupies roughly 64\*224\*224\*3\*4 bytes, about 38.5 MB, which is why image pipelines resize early rather than loading full-resolution originals into a batch. |
| **Worked example**      | Using OpenCV: gray = cv2.cvtColor(img, cv2.COLOR_RGB2GRAY) and hsv = cv2.cvtColor(img, cv2.COLOR_RGB2HSV). Resize the same image three ways: cv2.resize(img,(128,128),interpolation=cv2.INTER_NEAREST) vs INTER_LINEAR vs INTER_CUBIC, then stack five resized images into a batch with np.stack(\[...\], axis=0) and confirm the resulting shape is (5, 128, 128, 3).                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |

**Knowledge check:** Why must every image be resized to the same height and width before stacking them into a single batch tensor?

**(A) Because a tensor requires all elements along a given axis to have the same size**

\(B\) Because GPUs cannot process rectangular images, only square ones

\(C\) Because color channels only align correctly when height and width are equal

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Take five images of different original sizes, resize each to 128x128 using bilinear interpolation, convert to float32 tensors, and stack them into a single batch tensor; print the final shape and confirm it matches (5, 3, 128, 128) or (5, 128, 128, 3) depending on the convention you used.

**Lecture 471 Images/tensors**

*Year 3 · Month 28 · Computer Vision · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
|-------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Build a real image-loading pipeline with torchvision transforms, including normalization and augmentation, on an actual image dataset.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
| **Teacher explanation** | Real training pipelines rarely feed raw pixel tensors directly; torchvision.transforms (or an equivalent library) composes a sequence of operations such as Resize, RandomHorizontalFlip, RandomCrop, ToTensor, and Normalize. Normalization subtracts a per-channel mean and divides by a per-channel standard deviation; the widely used ImageNet statistics are mean=\[0.485, 0.456, 0.406\] and std=\[0.229, 0.224, 0.225\], so that pixel values entering the network are roughly zero-centered with unit variance, which stabilizes gradient-based optimization. Augmentations like random flips, crops, and color jitter are applied only during training, never during validation or test, because they intentionally introduce variation to reduce overfitting while evaluation must reflect the true, unaltered data distribution. We will work through a small folder of labeled images, build a torchvision.datasets.ImageFolder or a custom Dataset, and visualize a batch before and after normalization to confirm the pipeline behaves as intended. |
| **Worked example**      | train_tf = transforms.Compose(\[transforms.Resize((224,224)), transforms.RandomHorizontalFlip(), transforms.ToTensor(), transforms.Normalize(mean=\[0.485,0.456,0.406\], std=\[0.229,0.224,0.225\])\]); val_tf drops the RandomHorizontalFlip. Load a small folder dataset with ImageFolder(root, transform=train_tf) and print one normalized tensor's min and max values, which should now be roughly between -2 and 2, not 0 and 1.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |

**Knowledge check:** Why is random horizontal flip applied to the training set's transform but excluded from the validation set's transform?

**(A) Augmentation should vary the training data to reduce overfitting, but evaluation must measure performance on unaltered data**

\(B\) Flipping is only mathematically valid for square images, and validation images may not be square

\(C\) Validation sets are always too small to support any data augmentation

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Build a torchvision transform pipeline with resize, random flip, ToTensor, and ImageNet normalization; apply it to a small folder of at least 20 images split into train and val, and print the shape and value range of one batch from each split to confirm normalization took effect.

**Lecture 472 Images/tensors**

*Year 3 · Month 28 · Computer Vision · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
|-------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Diagnose and fix the most common image-tensor bugs: channel-order mismatches, forgotten normalization reversal, and incorrect axis permutation when visualizing.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
| **Teacher explanation** | The single most common bug in image pipelines is channel-order confusion: OpenCV loads images as BGR, not RGB, so displaying an OpenCV-loaded image with matplotlib without first converting via cv2.cvtColor(img, cv2.COLOR_BGR2RGB) produces an image with the red and blue channels swapped. A second common bug is visualizing a normalized tensor directly: because Normalize can push values outside \[0,1\], matplotlib's imshow will clip or wash out the image unless you first reverse the normalization by multiplying by std and adding mean, or clamp with torch.clamp. A third bug is forgetting to permute axes before display: a PyTorch tensor of shape (C, H, W) must be permuted to (H, W, C) with .permute(1,2,0) before imshow, otherwise matplotlib raises a shape error or renders nonsense. A fourth, subtler bug is dtype overflow during manual pixel arithmetic on uint8 arrays: adding 200 to a pixel already at 100 wraps around to 44 instead of saturating at 255, because uint8 arithmetic is modular, so such operations should be done in a wider dtype such as int16 or float32 before clipping back. |
| **Worked example**      | Reproduce and fix each bug in turn: load with cv2.imread and show directly versus after cvtColor(BGR2RGB); take a normalized tensor and call imshow directly (washed out), then unnormalize with img\*std + mean before showing; take a (3,224,224) tensor, call imshow(tensor) (error), then fix with imshow(tensor.permute(1,2,0)); create a uint8 array of value 200, add 100 with uint8 arithmetic and observe wraparound versus casting to int16 first.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |

**Knowledge check:** A PyTorch image tensor has shape (3, 224, 224). Calling plt.imshow(tensor) directly raises an error or shows garbage. What is the correct fix?

**(A) Permute the tensor to shape (224, 224, 3) before passing it to imshow**

\(B\) Convert the tensor to a plain Python list before passing it to imshow

\(C\) Multiply every value in the tensor by 255 before passing it to imshow

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Take one image you loaded with OpenCV and one you normalized with torchvision, and write a short script that correctly displays both using matplotlib, fixing the BGR/RGB swap in the first and reversing normalization plus permuting axes in the second.

Build train_loader = DataLoader(train_ds, batch_size=32, shuffle=True, num_workers=2) and val_loader = DataLoader(val_ds, batch_size=32, shuffle=False); pull imgs, labels = next(iter(train_loader)) and print imgs.shape, imgs.dtype, labels.shape.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |

**Knowledge check:** In a DataLoader, why is shuffle=True used for the training set but shuffle=False for the validation set?

**(A) Shuffling training batches prevents the model from learning spurious order-dependent patterns, while validation order does not affect the metric and keeping it fixed aids debugging**

\(B\) Validation data is always too small to be shuffled correctly

**Lecture 474 CNN concepts**

*Year 3 · Month 28 · Computer Vision · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
|-------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Explain the convolution operation itself, including kernels, stride, and padding, and compute the output size of a conv layer by hand.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
| **Teacher explanation** | A convolutional layer slides a small learnable filter, typically 3x3 or 5x5, across the input, computing a dot product at each position to produce a feature map; unlike a fully connected layer, the same kernel weights are reused at every spatial position, which gives CNNs translation invariance and a drastically smaller parameter count than a dense layer over the same input. Stride controls how far the kernel moves between applications: stride 1 produces an output nearly the same size as the input, stride 2 roughly halves each spatial dimension, and padding, commonly zero-padding chosen to preserve size, controls whether the output shrinks at the borders or stays the same size as the input. The output spatial size follows out = floor((in + 2\*padding - kernel) / stride) + 1, so a 32x32 input with a 3x3 kernel, stride 1, and padding 1 produces a 32x32 output, while the same kernel with no padding produces 30x30. Each kernel produces one output channel, and a conv layer with 64 filters over a 3-channel input produces a 64-channel feature map, with each filter learning to detect a different local pattern such as an edge or a color gradient. |
| **Worked example**      | Compute by hand: input 28x28x1, kernel 5x5, stride 1, padding 0 gives out = floor((28+0-5)/1)+1 = 24, so the output is 24x24. Implement it with conv = nn.Conv2d(in_channels=1, out_channels=16, kernel_size=5, stride=1, padding=0), pass a dummy torch.randn(1,1,28,28) through it, and confirm conv(x).shape equals (1,16,24,24).                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |

**Knowledge check:** A 3x3 kernel is applied to a 10x10x1 input with stride 1 and padding 0. What is the resulting output height and width?

**(A) 8x8**

\(B\) 10x10

\(C\) 7x7

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** By hand, compute the output spatial size for three different kernel/stride/padding combinations on a 32x32 input, then verify each with nn.Conv2d and a dummy tensor, printing the actual shape next to your hand-calculated prediction.

**Lecture 475 CNN concepts**

*Year 3 · Month 28 · Computer Vision · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
|-------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Explain pooling, receptive field growth across layers, and 1x1 convolutions, and why stacking small kernels can replace one large kernel.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
| **Teacher explanation** | Pooling layers downsample feature maps by taking the max or mean over small non-overlapping windows, typically 2x2 with stride 2, reducing spatial dimensions by half while keeping the number of channels unchanged; max pooling tends to preserve the strongest activation, useful for detecting whether a feature is present anywhere in a region, while average pooling smooths. The receptive field is the region of the original input that influences a given output unit, and it grows with depth: a single 3x3 conv layer has a 3x3 receptive field, but stacking two 3x3 conv layers gives a 5x5 effective receptive field at roughly half the parameters of one 5x5 conv layer, 2\*3\*3=18 weights per channel pair versus 25, which is why modern architectures favor stacks of small 3x3 kernels over large kernels. A 1x1 convolution does not look at any spatial neighborhood at all; it only mixes information across channels at each pixel, and is used to cheaply change the number of channels, for example reducing 256 channels to 64 before an expensive 3x3 conv, a trick central to bottleneck blocks in ResNet and Inception. |
| **Worked example**      | Build a tiny stack: nn.Sequential(nn.Conv2d(3,16,3,padding=1), nn.ReLU(), nn.Conv2d(16,16,3,padding=1), nn.ReLU(), nn.MaxPool2d(2)) on a 32x32x3 input, and trace the shape after each layer: 32x32x16, then 32x32x16, then 16x16x16. Then show that a 1x1 conv nn.Conv2d(16, 4, 1) changes only the channel count, leaving the spatial dims at 16x16.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |

**Knowledge check:** Why do two stacked 3x3 convolutional layers achieve roughly the same receptive field as a single 5x5 convolution while using fewer parameters per output channel?

**(A) Because 2 times 3x3 equals 18 weights versus 5x5 equals 25 weights for the single larger kernel, and the stack also adds a nonlinearity in between**

\(B\) Because 3x3 kernels always run faster on GPU hardware regardless of parameter count

\(C\) Because pooling is automatically inserted between every convolution by default

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Build two small networks on the same 32x32 input, one with a single 5x5 conv layer and one with two stacked 3x3 conv layers, count each network's total parameters with sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters()), and compare the two totals.
