| **Learning outcome**    | Define and distinguish data drift, concept drift, and label drift as the three categories of distributional change affecting a deployed model.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| **Teacher explanation** | Drift refers to any change over time in the statistical relationships a model was trained to exploit, and distinguishing its type matters because each requires a different response. Data drift (also called covariate shift) is a change in the distribution of the input features themselves, independent of their relationship to the target — e.g., a sudden shift in customer age distribution due to a new marketing campaign reaching a younger audience, even if 'how age relates to churn' hasn't changed. Concept drift is a change in the actual relationship between inputs and the target — the same input now leads to a different outcome, e.g., pre-pandemic versus pandemic-era relationships between income and spending behavior genuinely changed, not just the input distribution. Label drift is a change in the distribution of the target variable itself over time, e.g., the overall fraud rate doubling due to a new attack pattern, which can happen independently of both input drift and concept drift. Confusing these matters in practice: data drift alone, with the input-output relationship unchanged, might not require retraining at all if the model generalizes fine to the new input range, while concept drift almost always requires retraining because the learned relationship is now stale. |
| **Worked example**      | A retail demand-forecasting model trained pre-pandemic experiences: data drift (online order volume share increased, changing the input feature distribution), concept drift (the relationship between 'promotional discount %' and 'units sold' changed because consumer price sensitivity shifted during the pandemic), and label drift (the overall average units-sold target shifted upward due to e-commerce growth) — all three can be happening simultaneously but point to different root causes and different fixes.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |

**Knowledge check:** Why does distinguishing data drift from concept drift matter practically, rather than just noting 'something changed'?

\(A\) They always require the identical fix, so the distinction is purely academic

**(B) Data drift (input distribution changed, relationship intact) may not require retraining if the model generalizes well, while concept drift (the input-output relationship itself changed) almost always requires retraining since the learned pattern is stale**

\(C\) Concept drift can only happen in time-series models

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** For a model or dataset you're familiar with, construct one plausible hypothetical example each of data drift, concept drift, and label drift, explaining in one sentence per example what specifically changed.

**Lecture 566 drift**

*Year 3 · Month 33 · MLOps · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
|-------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Apply statistical tests for drift detection — population stability index (PSI), the Kolmogorov-Smirnov test, and KL divergence — and interpret their outputs.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
| **Teacher explanation** | Having defined drift types conceptually (lecture 565), we now quantify them. The Population Stability Index (PSI), widely used in credit risk modeling, bins a feature's values (using the reference/training distribution's bin edges) and compares the proportion of current data falling in each bin against the reference proportion, summing a weighted log-ratio across bins; conventional thresholds are PSI \< 0.1 (no significant shift), 0.1-0.25 (moderate shift, worth investigating), and \> 0.25 (significant shift, action likely needed). The Kolmogorov-Smirnov (KS) test is a non-parametric statistical test comparing two empirical cumulative distribution functions, producing a test statistic (the maximum distance between the two CDFs) and a p-value for whether the two samples come from the same underlying distribution — useful for continuous features without needing to choose bins. KL (Kullback-Leibler) divergence measures how one probability distribution diverges from a reference distribution in information-theoretic terms (bits of information lost if you assumed the reference distribution when the true one is current); unlike PSI and KS, KL divergence is asymmetric (KL(P\|\|Q) != KL(Q\|\|P)) which matters when choosing which distribution is the 'reference.' |
| **Worked example**      | PSI in Python: bin both reference and current feature values into the same 10 bins, compute \`psi = sum((current_pct - ref_pct) \* np.log(current_pct / ref_pct))\` across bins. For a 'transaction_amount' feature, PSI=0.31 signals significant drift worth investigating, while \`scipy.stats.ks_2samp(reference_amounts, current_amounts)\` returning a p-value of 0.002 independently confirms the two distributions are very unlikely to be the same, corroborating the PSI finding with a different statistical method.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |

**Knowledge check:** A feature's PSI value comes out to 0.31. According to conventional PSI interpretation thresholds, what does this indicate?

\(A\) No significant distribution shift; no action needed

**(B) A significant distributional shift that likely warrants investigation or action**

\(C\) The feature has exactly 31% missing values

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Compute PSI by hand or in Python for a feature comparing a reference sample to a deliberately shifted current sample, and separately run a Kolmogorov-Smirnov test on the same two samples, comparing the conclusions each method gives.

**Lecture 567 drift**

*Year 3 · Month 33 · MLOps · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
|-------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Detect drift in a realistic simulated dataset using Evidently or river, distinguishing genuine drift from seasonal or cyclical variation.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
| **Teacher explanation** | This hands-on lecture applies drift detection tooling (building on the monitoring dashboard work from lecture 563) to a dataset with deliberately simulated distribution shift, while also addressing a critical practical pitfall: seasonality can look exactly like drift to a naive detector. We construct a synthetic retail dataset where a feature ('average basket size') has genuine weekly seasonality (higher on weekends) layered with an injected true drift (a gradual upward trend over 3 months representing real customer behavior change) and show that a naive day-over-day PSI check fires false alarms every weekend. The fix is comparing the current window against a reference window from the same phase of the cycle (weekend-to-weekend, not weekend-to-weekday), or using a seasonal decomposition (e.g., \`statsmodels.tsa.seasonal_decompose\`) to separate the trend component from the seasonal component before running drift tests only on the trend. We also use the streaming \`river\` library's incremental drift detectors (ADWIN, DDM) as an alternative to batch-based PSI/KS, which continuously track a performance signal and flag the specific point where a change is detected, suited to high-volume streaming scenarios where recomputing a full batch report is too slow. |
| **Worked example**      | Naive check: comparing Monday's average basket size to the training reference (collected across all days) fires a false drift alarm every single Monday because Mondays are structurally different from the mixed-day reference. Fixed check: compare this Monday's basket size distribution only against the reference's Monday-only subset, or run \`seasonal_decompose(series, period=7)\` and monitor only the \`.trend\` component for drift, correctly letting the weekly cycle through without alarm while still catching the true 3-month upward trend.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |

**Knowledge check:** Why might a naive day-over-day drift check on a feature with strong weekly seasonality produce frequent false alarms?

\(A\) Drift detection methods always fail on retail data specifically

**(B) The naive check compares against a reference that mixes all days together, so a day with a structurally different normal pattern (e.g., weekends) looks like drift relative to that mixed reference even with no real behavior change**

\(C\) Seasonal data cannot be analyzed with any statistical method

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Construct a synthetic time series with both weekly seasonality and an injected gradual trend, run a naive drift check comparing arbitrary windows, observe the false alarms, then apply seasonal decomposition and re-run drift detection only on the trend component, comparing the results.

**Lecture 568 drift**

*Year 3 · Month 33 · MLOps · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
|-------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Identify and avoid common drift-detection mistakes: oversensitive thresholds, ignoring feature correlation structure, and conflating drift with data pipeline bugs.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
| **Teacher explanation** | Drift detection, like monitoring alerting (lecture 564), is prone to a few recurring mistakes beyond the seasonality trap from lecture 567. Oversensitive thresholds (e.g., treating any PSI above 0.05 as actionable) generate so many false alarms that the team starts ignoring drift reports entirely — thresholds should be validated against a known-stable historical period first, to calibrate what 'normal' noise looks like for that specific feature and dataset, rather than importing a generic textbook cutoff unchanged. Ignoring correlation structure means checking each feature's marginal distribution independently can miss drift in the joint relationship between features even when each one's individual distribution looks stable — e.g., two features that used to be strongly correlated (income and loan amount) becoming decorrelated is a real and important shift that marginal PSI checks per feature will not detect, requiring either a multivariate drift test or explicit monitoring of key feature-pair correlations. Finally, a large apparent 'drift' event is very often not drift at all but a silent data pipeline bug — a schema change, a null-filling default suddenly applied upstream, a timezone bug shifting all timestamps by hours — so any strong drift signal should first be cross-checked against recent upstream pipeline changes before being treated as a genuine real-world behavior shift requiring retraining. |
| **Worked example**      | Postmortem: a sudden PSI spike to 0.9 on a 'transaction_hour' feature looked like dramatic drift, triggering a retraining effort, until someone noticed an upstream ETL change had switched the timestamp column from UTC to local time that same week — the 'drift' was a pipeline bug, not a real behavior change, and retraining on it would have baked in a confusing artifact rather than fixing anything. The team added a standing check: any drift alert above a high-severity threshold now automatically also runs against the upstream pipeline's recent changelog before anyone starts a retrain.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |

**Knowledge check:** Before concluding that a large, sudden drift signal reflects genuine real-world behavior change requiring retraining, what should be checked first?

\(A\) Whether the model's file size has changed

**(B) Whether a recent upstream data pipeline change (schema, timezone, null-handling) could be the actual cause rather than real behavioral drift**

\(C\) Nothing; any drift signal should trigger immediate retraining without further investigation

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Review (or construct) a drift alert scenario, and write a short investigation checklist of upstream pipeline changes (schema changes, timezone handling, default value changes) you would check before concluding the signal represents genuine behavioral drift.

**Lecture 569 retraining**

*Year 3 · Month 33 · MLOps · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
|-------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Design retraining triggers and compare scheduled retraining against drift-triggered and performance-triggered retraining strategies.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               |
| **Teacher explanation** | Having established how to detect drift (lectures 565-568) and monitor performance (561-564), this lecture addresses what to actually do about it: when should a model be retrained? Scheduled retraining runs on a fixed calendar cadence (e.g., weekly or monthly) regardless of whether drift has been detected, which is simple to implement and reason about but can retrain unnecessarily (wasting compute and risking instability if a retrain, by chance, produces a slightly worse model from noise) or too infrequently (if drift happens faster than the schedule). Drift-triggered retraining instead fires automatically when a drift detector (lecture 566-567) crosses a defined threshold, aligning retraining effort with actual need, but requires the drift detection pipeline itself to be reliable and well-tuned (lecture 568's mistakes directly undermine this if unaddressed) and needs a cooldown/debounce period so a single noisy spike doesn't trigger a flurry of retrains. Performance-triggered retraining fires based on the ground-truth-based quality metrics from lecture 562 dropping below a threshold, which is the most directly business-relevant trigger but suffers from the ground-truth delay problem — by the time a performance drop is confirmed, damage may already have accumulated, making it best used in combination with the earlier-warning drift trigger rather than alone. |
| **Worked example**      | A fraud model uses a layered trigger strategy: scheduled monthly retraining as a baseline floor, PLUS an automatic drift-triggered retrain if any of three key features exceeds PSI 0.25 for 3 consecutive days (with a 7-day cooldown to avoid retrain storms), PLUS an escalated/expedited retrain if confirmed fraud-catch-rate (ground truth, delayed) drops below 85%. This layered approach catches both slow drift (via schedule) and fast-moving drift (via the PSI trigger) while treating confirmed performance drops as the most urgent signal.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |

**Knowledge check:** Why might a team combine drift-triggered retraining with performance-triggered retraining rather than relying on performance metrics alone?

\(A\) Performance metrics are never useful for ML systems

**(B) Drift signals are available earlier than performance metrics due to the ground-truth delay, so combining both catches problems sooner than waiting for confirmed performance degradation alone**

\(C\) Drift-triggered retraining requires no monitoring infrastructure at all

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Design a retraining trigger strategy for a model of your choice that combines at least two of (scheduled, drift-triggered, performance-triggered) retraining, specifying the exact thresholds and any cooldown period, and justify the combination in two sentences.

**Lecture 570 retraining**

*Year 3 · Month 33 · MLOps · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
|-------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Explain the champion/challenger pattern and shadow testing as a safe rollout strategy for a newly retrained model before full production replacement.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       |
| **Teacher explanation** | Once a retraining trigger (lecture 569) produces a new candidate model, replacing the current production model outright is risky — offline evaluation metrics, even when good, don't guarantee production behavior (echoing the shadow deployment rationale from lecture 562). The champion/challenger pattern formalizes a safer rollout: the current production model is the 'champion,' and each newly retrained candidate is a 'challenger' that must prove itself against the champion on real traffic before earning promotion. This typically proceeds through shadow testing first (the challenger receives a copy of live traffic and its predictions are logged but never shown to users, exactly as in lecture 562), then a canary/gradual rollout where the challenger is given a small percentage of real decision-making traffic (e.g., 5%) while being closely monitored against the champion's established baseline metrics, and only promoted to become the new champion (via the registry's stage transition from lecture 559) if it meets or beats the champion on the monitored metrics over a defined evaluation window, with an automatic rollback path if the challenger underperforms at any stage. |
| **Worked example**      | Rollout sequence for a newly retrained recommendation model: Day 1-3, shadow mode (challenger logs predictions, 0% real traffic exposure, compared offline against champion's historical predictions on the same requests); Day 4-7, 5% canary (challenger makes real recommendations for 5% of users, monitored for click-through rate versus champion's baseline); if click-through rate matches or exceeds the champion's with no guardrail-metric regression, promote to 50% for 3 more days, then 100%, formally becoming the new champion in the registry.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |

**Knowledge check:** In the champion/challenger pattern, what is the purpose of the shadow-testing phase specifically, before any canary/gradual rollout begins?

\(A\) Shadow testing is purely optional documentation with no functional purpose

**(B) Shadow testing exposes the challenger to real production traffic patterns with zero risk to real users, since its predictions are only logged and never actually used to make decisions**

\(C\) Shadow testing automatically promotes the model to production without further review

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Design a full champion/challenger rollout plan (shadow phase duration, canary percentage and duration, promotion criteria, and rollback condition) for a newly retrained model of your choice.

**Lecture 571 retraining**

*Year 3 · Month 33 · MLOps · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
|-------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Automate an end-to-end retraining pipeline with a workflow orchestrator and define a concrete rollback strategy, synthesizing the month's CI/CD, registry, monitoring, and drift concepts.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
| **Teacher explanation** | This closing, synthesis lecture for the retraining arc wires together every piece from the month into one automated pipeline using a workflow orchestrator (Airflow or Kubeflow Pipelines are the common choices; both let you define a directed acyclic graph of pipeline steps with dependencies, retries, and scheduling). The pipeline: a trigger (scheduled, drift-based, or performance-based, per lecture 569) kicks off a DAG that pulls the latest versioned data, runs the CI/CD-style quality-gated training and evaluation steps (lectures 553-556), registers the resulting model as a new version in Staging (lectures 557-559), automatically runs it through a shadow-test comparison against the current champion (lecture 570), and if the challenger passes, opens an approval gate for a human or automated promotion decision rather than auto-promoting to Production unconditionally — full automation of training is common, but most mature teams keep a deliberate human or strict automated-metric gate specifically at the final production promotion step. A rollback strategy is defined in advance, not improvised during an incident: the registry (lecture 557) always retains the previous production version, so reverting is a single stage-transition operation (promote the prior version back to Production, demote the failed one), and the monitoring dashboard (lecture 561-564) is what should trigger that rollback decision, closing the loop from detection back to action. |
| **Worked example**      | Airflow DAG sketch: \`pull_data \>\> validate_data \>\> train_model \>\> evaluate_model \>\> register_staging \>\> shadow_test \>\> \[approval_gate\] \>\> promote_to_production\`, with the \`evaluate_model\` and \`shadow_test\` tasks each able to short-circuit the DAG (mark downstream tasks as skipped/failed) if their respective quality gates aren't met, and a separate, always-available \`rollback_to_previous_version\` task that an on-call engineer can trigger manually by reading the previous production version directly from the registry's version history.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |

**Knowledge check:** Why do most mature MLOps teams keep a deliberate approval gate at the final production-promotion step, even when every earlier pipeline stage (training, evaluation, shadow testing) is fully automated?

\(A\) Automation of the promotion step is technically impossible

**(B) A final human or strict automated gate at the point of highest consequence (replacing the live production model) catches issues that automated metrics alone might miss, before the irreversible step of affecting real users**

\(C\) Approval gates are only a legal requirement in some countries, not a technical best practice

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Sketch a full Airflow-or-Kubeflow-style DAG for an automated retraining pipeline (listing every stage from data pull through production promotion with at least one explicit gate), and separately write out the exact rollback procedure you would follow if the newly promoted model caused a regression.

**Lecture 572 Month 33 Examination**

*Year 3 · Month 33 · MLOps · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               |
|-------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Demonstrate integrated mastery of CI/CD for ML, model registries, monitoring, drift detection, and retraining concepts covered this month.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
| **Teacher explanation** | This review lecture consolidates the month's five teaching arcs across this 20-hour month. From CI/CD for ML, we revisit why ML pipelines must version data and models alongside code, the ML-specific testing pyramid (unit, data validation, behavioral tests), building a quality-gated GitHub Actions workflow, and diagnosing environment non-reproducibility and flaky pipelines. From model registries, we revisit lifecycle stages, the MLflow registry API and lineage tracing, a full promotion worked example, and comparisons across MLflow/SageMaker/Vertex AI registries. From monitoring, we revisit operational versus model-quality metrics, prediction-logging and shadow-deployment architecture, building an Evidently dashboard, and calibrating alert thresholds including segment-level breakdowns. From drift, we revisit data/concept/label drift definitions, PSI/KS/KL divergence statistical tests, distinguishing true drift from seasonality, and avoiding oversensitive thresholds or mistaking pipeline bugs for drift. From retraining, we revisit scheduled versus drift- versus performance-triggered retraining, the champion/challenger pattern with shadow and canary phases, and a fully automated retraining DAG with an explicit rollback strategy. There is no external certification tied to this month; consistent with the rest of the program, the internal passing standard for this examination is 80%, and students should be able to both execute concrete steps (write a quality-gated CI step, compute PSI) and reason through end-to-end system design (how a drift signal should flow through monitoring into a retraining trigger into a champion/challenger rollout). |
| **Worked example**      | Comprehensive practice set: (1) write a GitHub Actions quality-gate step pseudocode for a training pipeline; (2) given a registry lineage query, trace a production model back to its data version; (3) compute PSI for a given reference/current distribution pair and interpret it; (4) design a full trigger-to-rollout pipeline (drift detection -\> retraining trigger -\> champion/challenger rollout -\> rollback plan) for a given scenario.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |

**Knowledge check:** This exam covers five topic arcs from the month. Which pairing correctly matches a concept to its arc?

\(A\) The champion/challenger pattern belongs to CI/CD for ML; PSI belongs to model registries

**(B) Shadow deployment logging belongs to monitoring; the Population Stability Index (PSI) belongs to drift detection**

\(C\) MLflow's registry API belongs to drift; Great Expectations data validation belongs to retraining

***Correct answer: B***

**Homework:** Complete the full practice exam set covering a CI quality-gate step, a registry lineage trace, a PSI computation and interpretation, and an end-to-end trigger-to-rollout pipeline design, targeting at least 80% correct to complete Month 33 and the MLOps arc of the program.
