**Lecture 607 Problem**

*Year 3 · Month 36 · Final Data Science & AI Capstone · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
|-------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Evaluate three candidate capstone problem statements side by side and justify selecting one over the others.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
| **Teacher explanation** | With three well-formed candidates in hand, the final choice is a deliberate trade-off, not a coin flip: weigh data availability and quality, how much of the program's breadth each lets you demonstrate, personal interest (a 20-hour solo build goes better on a problem you actually want to finish), and how defensible the result will be in an interview setting from Month 35. Walking through this comparison explicitly, in writing, is itself the skill — it mirrors exactly the kind of prioritization decision a working data scientist makes when a manager hands them three possible projects and a limited quarter.                                                      |
| **Worked example**      | Comparison table: Candidate A (hospital readmission, public CMS-style dataset) — data quality high, breadth high (pipeline+stats+ML+deployment), interest high. Candidate B (e-commerce demand forecasting, synthetic) — data quality medium (self-generated, less externally defensible in an interview), breadth medium (time series heavy, lighter on deployment). Candidate C (credit card fraud detection, public Kaggle dataset) — data quality high, breadth medium (strong ML, weaker natural fit for the communication/stakeholder narrative). Decision: Candidate A selected for the strongest combination of real data, full-lifecycle breadth, and interview defensibility. |

**Knowledge check:** When choosing among several well-formed capstone candidates, why does 'how defensible the result will be in an interview' matter as a selection criterion?

**(A) Because the capstone becomes a key piece of interview material, a project built on real, explainable data holds up better under follow-up questions than one on data whose quality can't be vouched for**

\(B\) Because interviewers only accept projects using data from certain approved providers

\(C\) It doesn't matter — any completed capstone is equally useful in an interview

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Write a comparison table for your own 2-3 candidate capstone problems across data quality, breadth, interest, and interview defensibility, and justify your final choice in writing.

**Lecture 608 Problem**

*Year 3 · Month 36 · Final Data Science & AI Capstone · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
|-------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Diagnose common capstone-scoping mistakes and use a scoping worksheet to narrow an overly broad topic into a buildable project.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
| **Teacher explanation** | The most common capstone-scoping mistakes are: too broad ('analyze healthcare data' has no edges), no clear metric (restating Month 34's lesson one more time because it's the single most frequent real-world failure), and unavailable data (choosing a problem that sounds great but whose real dataset requires an institutional agreement you don't have). The fix is a scoping worksheet with forced constraints: one dataset, one population, one decision, one metric, one deployment target — filled in before any code is written, and revisited if any answer is still vague after a first pass.                                    |
| **Worked example**      | Worksheet filled in for a student who started with 'I want to analyze healthcare data to improve patient outcomes': Dataset -\> narrowed to a specific public discharge-summary dataset with a known schema. Population -\> adult patients discharged from a medical (not surgical) unit. Decision -\> which patients get a prioritized follow-up call. Metric -\> recall at a cost-weighted threshold, benchmarked against discharge-order prioritization. Deployment target -\> a simple scored CSV + a one-page Streamlit lookup tool, not a real-time hospital system integration (correctly ruled out of scope for a 20-hour solo build). |

**Knowledge check:** Why is 'ruling out real-time integration with a live hospital system' a correct scoping decision for this capstone, rather than a cop-out?

**(A) It matches the problem's actual constraints (solo build, ~20 hours, no production access) while still fully answering the stated decision with a lighter-weight deployment target**

\(B\) Real-time systems are never appropriate for any data science project

\(C\) Hospitals do not allow any software projects involving patient data under any circumstances

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Fill out the one-dataset/one-population/one-decision/one-metric/one-deployment-target worksheet for your own chosen capstone problem.

**Lecture 609 data pipeline**

*Year 3 · Month 36 · Final Data Science & AI Capstone · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
|-------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Design a capstone-scale data pipeline architecture reusing the raw-staging-processed pattern from Month 18/19/30, sized appropriately for a solo 20-hour build.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
| **Teacher explanation** | The capstone pipeline reuses the exact architecture taught across the program's data engineering months — raw (untouched source extract), staging (typed and deduped), processed (final modeling table) — but the scale decision matters: a solo capstone does not need Spark or a distributed orchestrator; a well-structured set of Python scripts or a lightweight Airflow DAG run locally is the right-sized choice, and over-engineering the infrastructure at the expense of the analysis and model is a common capstone mistake examiners watch for. The discipline from earlier months carries over unchanged: nothing in processed/ is hand-edited, and every transformation step is a function, not a notebook cell. |
| **Worked example**      | Capstone pipeline for the readmission dataset: \`data/raw/discharge_records.csv\` (never touched) -\> \`src/pipeline.py\` with \`clean_demographics()\`, \`clean_diagnosis_codes()\`, \`build_modeling_table()\` -\> \`data/processed/readmission_modeling_table.parquet\`. No Spark cluster, no orchestrator beyond a single \`make pipeline\` command — right-sized for the actual data volume (tens of thousands of rows, not billions).                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |

**Knowledge check:** Why would introducing a distributed processing framework like Spark typically be the wrong choice for a solo 20-hour capstone on a dataset of tens of thousands of rows?

**(A) The added infrastructure complexity isn't justified by the data volume and would consume build time better spent on analysis, modeling, and communication**

\(B\) Spark cannot process any dataset smaller than one billion rows

\(C\) Distributed frameworks are banned from capstone projects by this program's rules

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Sketch your capstone's raw/staging/processed pipeline architecture and justify, in one sentence, why your chosen tooling is appropriately sized for your data volume.

**Lecture 610 data pipeline**

*Year 3 · Month 36 · Final Data Science & AI Capstone · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
|-------------------------|-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Implement explicit data quality checks — schema validation, null-rate thresholds, and outlier flags — inside the capstone pipeline, with logging.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
| **Teacher explanation** | A capstone pipeline earns credibility by proving the data was checked, not just transformed. Three concrete checks: schema validation (expected columns and types present, as in Month 34's pipeline run), null-rate thresholds (flag and report if any feature exceeds, say, 10% missing, rather than silently imputing and hoping), and outlier flags (a simple IQR or z-score check on key numeric features, logged for manual review rather than auto-dropped, since a true outlier in healthcare data — a 95-year-old with 40 prior admissions — may be a real and important case, not noise). All three checks run automatically on every pipeline execution and produce a short data-quality report alongside the processed table. |
| **Worked example**      | \`\`\`python def data_quality_report(df: pd.DataFrame) -\> dict: report = {} for col in df.columns: null_rate = df\[col\].isna().mean() if null_rate \> 0.10: report\[col\] = f'WARNING: {null_rate:.1%} missing' numeric_cols = df.select_dtypes('number').columns for col in numeric_cols: q1, q3 = df\[col\].quantile(\[0.25, 0.75\]) iqr = q3 - q1 outliers = df\[(df\[col\] \< q1 - 3\*iqr) \| (df\[col\] \> q3 + 3\*iqr)\] if len(outliers): report\[f'{col}\_outliers'\] = len(outliers) return report \`\`\`                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |

**Knowledge check:** Why does this lecture recommend logging outliers for manual review rather than automatically dropping them?

**(A) A statistical outlier can represent a real and important case (e.g. an unusually high-risk patient) rather than a data error, so automatic removal risks discarding exactly the cases that matter most**

\(B\) Dropping any row automatically is technically impossible in pandas

\(C\) Outliers never affect model performance, so there is no need to handle them at all

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Implement a data-quality report function (schema, null-rate, outlier checks) for your capstone pipeline and review its output before proceeding to analysis.

**Lecture 611 data pipeline**

*Year 3 · Month 36 · Final Data Science & AI Capstone · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
|-------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Build the complete capstone ingestion-to-modeling-table pipeline end to end for the chosen dataset.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |
| **Teacher explanation** | This is the capstone's actual pipeline build, run start to finish: load the raw discharge dataset, apply the data-quality checks from 610, clean and standardize (diagnosis codes mapped to a smaller set of categories, dates parsed consistently, demographic fields standardized), and output one versioned modeling table with a derived target column (readmitted_30d) computed correctly and leakage-checked using Month 34's leakage-audit habit — no column that is only populated after the readmission event is allowed to remain as a feature.      |
| **Worked example**      | \`\`\`python df = pd.read_csv('data/raw/discharge_records.csv') report = data_quality_report(df) print(report) df\['readmitted_30d'\] = ( (df\['readmission_date'\] - df\['discharge_date'\]).dt.days.between(0, 30) ).astype(int) leakage_risk = \[c for c in df.columns if 'readmission' in c.lower() and c != 'readmitted_30d'\] assert not leakage_risk, f'Potential leakage columns: {leakage_risk}' df_model = df.drop(columns=\['readmission_date'\] + leakage_risk) df_model.to_parquet('data/processed/readmission_modeling_table_v1.parquet') \`\`\` |

**Knowledge check:** In this pipeline, why is the raw 'readmission_date' column dropped from the final modeling table even though it was used to compute the target?

**(A) Keeping the raw event-timing column itself (or anything derived only from post-outcome information) in the feature set would leak the answer into the model's inputs**

\(B\) Date columns are never allowed in any pandas dataframe used for modeling

\(C\) It takes up too much disk space to keep as a column

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Build your capstone's complete pipeline end to end, including a leakage audit on the final feature set before moving to analysis.

**Lecture 612 analysis**

*Year 3 · Month 36 · Final Data Science & AI Capstone · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
|-------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Plan and execute an exploratory data analysis pass on the capstone modeling table, covering univariate, bivariate, and missingness patterns.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
| **Teacher explanation** | EDA on the capstone dataset follows a deliberate order: univariate first (distribution of age, length of stay, diagnosis category — catching skew and impossible values like a negative length of stay before any comparison is trusted), then bivariate (how does the readmission rate vary by diagnosis category, by age band, by number of prior admissions), then a missingness pattern check (is missingness random, or does it cluster — e.g. insurance-type data missing disproportionately for one hospital site, which would bias any conclusion drawn from that field). Skipping straight to bivariate analysis without the univariate pass is how a capstone ends up reporting a dramatic-looking relationship that's actually driven by three corrupted rows. |
| **Worked example**      | Univariate check catches a real issue: \`df.length_of_stay.describe()\` shows a minimum of -3 — impossible, traced to a data entry error in 40 rows (0.3% of the dataset), fixed by filtering before any further analysis. Bivariate finding, now trustworthy: readmission rate is 34% for patients with 3+ prior admissions versus 9% for patients with zero prior admissions — a 3.8x difference. Missingness check: insurance_type is missing 22% of the time, but only for one hospital site, flagged as a sampling bias risk to disclose rather than impute away silently.                                                                                                                                                                                           |

**Knowledge check:** Why does univariate analysis need to happen before bivariate analysis in this EDA workflow, rather than afterward?

**(A) Catching data errors (like an impossible negative length-of-stay) before comparing groups prevents a corrupted handful of rows from producing a misleading bivariate finding**

\(B\) Univariate analysis is required by a specific Python library function ordering

\(C\) Bivariate analysis cannot technically run before univariate analysis in pandas

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Run a univariate pass on your capstone dataset's key fields, fix any impossible values found, then proceed to at least two bivariate comparisons.

**Lecture 613 analysis**

*Year 3 · Month 36 · Final Data Science & AI Capstone · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
|-------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Validate capstone EDA findings with a hypothesis test and confidence interval, rather than reporting raw percentage differences alone.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               |
| **Teacher explanation** | A bivariate difference like '34% versus 9% readmission rate' needs a statistical check before it goes in the final report, exactly as practiced in Month 34: is a difference this large plausible by chance given the sample sizes involved? A two-proportion z-test (or chi-square, for more than two groups) on readmission rate by prior-admission group gives a p-value, and a 95% confidence interval on the difference gives a plausible range rather than a single misleadingly precise number. Reporting '34% vs 9%, p\<0.001, 95% CI for the difference \[21%, 29%\]' is a materially stronger and more honest claim than '34% vs 9%' alone, which implies false precision. |
| **Worked example**      | \`\`\`python from statsmodels.stats.proportion import proportions_ztest, confint_proportions_2indep count = \[high_prior_readmits, low_prior_readmits\] nobs = \[n_high_prior, n_low_prior\] stat, pval = proportions_ztest(count, nobs) \# pval \< 0.001 ci_low, ci_high = confint_proportions_2indep(count\[0\], nobs\[0\], count\[1\], nobs\[1\]) \# e.g. (0.21, 0.29) -- the true difference is very likely in this range \`\`\`                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |

**Knowledge check:** What does reporting a 95% confidence interval add on top of a p-value when presenting a group difference?

**(A) It gives a plausible range for the size of the true difference, rather than only a yes/no signal about statistical significance**

\(B\) Confidence intervals replace the need for any sample size reporting

\(C\) A confidence interval proves the finding will replicate in every future dataset with certainty

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Run a two-proportion (or chi-square) test and compute a confidence interval for one bivariate finding in your capstone analysis, and report both numbers together.

**Lecture 614 analysis**

*Year 3 · Month 36 · Final Data Science & AI Capstone · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
|-------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Produce the capstone's key findings table and chart with a written interpretation tied directly back to the problem statement from lecture 606.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
| **Teacher explanation** | The analysis phase ends with the same discipline taught in Month 34, lecture 584: one table, one chart, one interpretation sentence, chosen because it answers the specific decision named in the problem statement — not because it's the most interesting pattern in the dataset. If the problem statement says the decision is 'which patients get prioritized follow-up calls,' the headline chart should show readmission rate by the segment that will actually drive that prioritization (e.g. by prior-admission count), not an unrelated but visually striking pattern like readmission by day-of-week-of-discharge that doesn't change any decision. |
| **Worked example**      | Final analysis artifact: table showing readmission rate by prior-admission bucket (0: 9%, 1-2: 18%, 3+: 34%), chart highlighting the 3+ bucket in color per lecture 595's annotation principles, interpretation: 'Patients with 3 or more prior admissions are readmitted at nearly 4x the rate of first-time patients and make up a identifiable, prioritizable segment for care coordination follow-up — directly actionable under the original problem statement.'                                                                                                                                                                                          |

**Knowledge check:** Why would a visually striking pattern unrelated to the stated decision (e.g. readmission by day-of-week-of-discharge) be a poor choice for the capstone's headline chart, even if it's statistically real?

**(A) The headline chart should answer the specific decision in the problem statement, not just showcase the most visually interesting pattern found**

\(B\) Day-of-week data is never statistically valid in any analysis

\(C\) Charts involving dates are technically impossible to build in standard plotting libraries

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Produce your capstone's headline table and chart, confirming it directly answers the decision stated in your lecture 606 problem statement.

**Lecture 615 ML**

*Year 3 · Month 36 · Final Data Science & AI Capstone · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
|-------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Select a model family and build a baseline for the capstone's prediction task, with an explicit rationale tied to the problem's constraints.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| **Teacher explanation** | Model selection for the capstone should be justified, not default. For a readmission risk classification task with a mix of categorical and numeric features and a need for some interpretability (care coordination staff will ask 'why is this patient flagged'), a reasonable progression is: a logistic regression baseline (fast, interpretable coefficients, sets the bar), then a tree-based model (random forest or gradient boosting) if it meaningfully beats the baseline on the metric that matters — recall at the cost-weighted threshold, not raw accuracy, carrying forward Month 34's lesson. Choosing a deep learning approach here, on a dataset of tens of thousands of tabular rows, would be a mismatch between tool and problem — a mistake worth naming explicitly in the capstone write-up as evidence of judgment, not just execution. |
| **Worked example**      | Rationale written into the capstone notebook: 'Baseline: logistic regression (readmitted_30d ~ prior_admissions + age + diagnosis_category + length_of_stay), AUC 0.68, coefficients directly interpretable for the care coordination team. Candidate: gradient-boosted trees, AUC 0.76. Deep learning explicitly ruled out — tabular data of this size and feature count does not benefit from it, and would sacrifice the interpretability this project's stakeholders need.'                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |

**Knowledge check:** Why would deep learning typically be a poor model choice for this capstone's readmission-prediction task?

**(A) On tabular data of this size with a need for interpretability, tree-based or linear models are typically a better fit and deep learning adds complexity without a clear benefit**

\(B\) Deep learning cannot technically be applied to any classification problem

\(C\) Deep learning models are illegal to use in healthcare-adjacent projects

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Build a baseline model and one stronger candidate for your capstone task, writing an explicit one-paragraph rationale for both choices including why you ruled out at least one alternative.

**Lecture 616 ML**

*Year 3 · Month 36 · Final Data Science & AI Capstone · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |
|-------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Tune the capstone model with cross-validation sized appropriately to the dataset, avoiding leakage between folds and the held-out test set.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
| **Teacher explanation** | Hyperparameter tuning needs its own held-out structure: k-fold cross-validation on the training set only (the out-of-time or held-out test set from the problem's split, following Month 34's out-of-time discipline, is never touched during tuning), searching a small, justified grid rather than every possible combination (a capstone has limited build hours; a targeted grid search over 2-3 key hyperparameters beats an exhaustive search that eats the time budget without materially improving the result). A specific leakage risk at this stage: if any preprocessing step (like scaling or imputing medians) is fit on the full dataset before the cross-validation split, information from the validation folds leaks into training — all preprocessing fitting must happen inside each fold, typically via a pipeline object. |
| **Worked example**      | \`\`\`python from sklearn.model_selection import GridSearchCV from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline pipe = Pipeline(\[('impute', SimpleImputer(strategy='median')), ('model', GradientBoostingClassifier())\]) param_grid = {'model\_\_max_depth': \[3, 5, 7\], 'model\_\_n_estimators': \[100, 200\]} search = GridSearchCV(pipe, param_grid, scoring='recall', cv=5) search.fit(X_train, y_train) \# held-out test set still untouched \`\`\`                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                |

**Knowledge check:** Why must preprocessing steps like median imputation be fit inside each cross-validation fold (via a pipeline) rather than once on the full training set before splitting into folds?

**(A) Fitting on the full set before splitting lets information from each validation fold leak into the statistics used to preprocess it, biasing the cross-validation score**

\(B\) Pipelines are required by scikit-learn's licensing terms

\(C\) It makes the code run in fewer lines regardless of correctness

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Set up a cross-validated hyperparameter search for your capstone model using a pipeline that fits preprocessing within each fold, keeping your final test set untouched.

**Lecture 617 ML**

*Year 3 · Month 36 · Final Data Science & AI Capstone · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
|-------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Present the capstone's final model results against the baseline with a model card, including known limitations.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
| **Teacher explanation** | The capstone's modeling phase closes with a results walkthrough and a model card — a short, standard-format document stating what the model predicts, what data it was trained on, its performance metrics at the deployed threshold, and crucially its known limitations (e.g. trained on data from one health system and may not generalize to a different patient population or coding practice; does not account for social determinants of health not captured in the dataset). Naming limitations explicitly is not a weakness in the capstone — a reviewer who sees you've thought about where the model could fail trusts the parts that do work more, not less. |
| **Worked example**      | Model card excerpt: 'Model: gradient-boosted classifier, AUC 0.76 (vs. 0.68 logistic baseline), recall 0.69 at the deployed cost-weighted threshold. Trained on 45,000 discharge records from a single public dataset spanning 2021-2023. Known limitations: does not include social determinants of health (housing stability, transportation access) known from clinical literature to affect readmission; may not generalize to hospital systems with different patient demographics or coding conventions than the training data; threshold was tuned using an assumed cost ratio, not validated against actual care-coordination outcomes.'                         |

**Knowledge check:** Why does explicitly stating a model's known limitations in its model card strengthen, rather than weaken, the capstone presentation?

**(A) It demonstrates the kind of critical judgment and awareness of failure modes that reviewers specifically look for, increasing trust in the parts of the work that are solid**

\(B\) Limitations sections are only included to meet a word-count requirement

\(C\) Listing limitations is required by federal law for every machine learning project

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Write a model card for your capstone model including at least two specific, honest limitations rather than generic disclaimers.

**Lecture 618 deployment**

*Year 3 · Month 36 · Final Data Science & AI Capstone · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |
|-------------------------|------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Choose a deployment format for the capstone model — batch scoring script, REST API, or lightweight app — based on how the output will actually be used.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| **Teacher explanation** | Deployment choice should follow directly from the problem statement's decision, not from what's most impressive to build. If care coordinators review a prioritized list once a day, a batch scoring script that outputs a ranked CSV each morning is the right-sized solution — building a full real-time REST API for a once-daily batch decision is over-engineering that costs build hours without adding value. If the use case genuinely needs on-demand scoring (a new patient record triggers an immediate check), a lightweight REST API (FastAPI/Flask) fits. If the audience is non-technical and wants to explore results interactively, a simple Streamlit app showing risk scores and the top contributing factors per patient is often the best fit of all three for a capstone demo, because it doubles as the communication artifact for Month 36's final presentation. |
| **Worked example**      | Decision made and justified in the capstone write-up: 'Chosen: a daily batch scoring script (\`score_daily.py\`) producing a ranked CSV, plus a lightweight Streamlit app for the live demo, allowing care coordination staff and, for this capstone's presentation, interviewers to explore individual risk scores interactively. A full production REST API was explicitly scoped out — the actual decision (daily call-list prioritization) does not require real-time scoring.'                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |

**Knowledge check:** Why would building a full real-time REST API be the wrong deployment choice for a use case where the decision is only made once per day from a batch list?

**(A) It adds engineering complexity and build time disproportionate to a decision that doesn't require real-time scoring, a mismatch between tool and actual need**

\(B\) REST APIs cannot technically return predictions in batch form

\(C\) Real-time APIs are against this program's academic policy

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Decide and justify in writing which deployment format fits your capstone's actual decision cadence, and build the simplest version that satisfies it.

**Lecture 619 deployment**

*Year 3 · Month 36 · Final Data Science & AI Capstone · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
|-------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Containerize the capstone deployment with Docker and add basic model-versioning and drift-monitoring logging.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
| **Teacher explanation** | Operationalizing the chosen deployment means it can run somewhere other than your own laptop and that you'd notice if it started failing silently. A Dockerfile pins the Python version and dependencies exactly as in Month 35's repo-quality lecture, now wrapping the actual scoring script or Streamlit app so it runs identically anywhere. Basic versioning means the saved model artifact has a version tag and training date embedded (\`model_v1_2026-09-01.pkl\`), not an unversioned \`model.pkl\` silently overwritten each retrain. Basic drift monitoring, even at capstone scale, means logging the distribution of key input features and the model's output score distribution on each batch run, so a future run that looks statistically different from the training data is flagged rather than trusted blindly. |
| **Worked example**      | \`\`\`python import joblib, datetime model_version = f"model_v1\_{datetime.date.today()}" joblib.dump(model, f'models/{model_version}.pkl') \# drift check on each new batch current_mean_age = new_batch.age.mean() training_mean_age = 58.3 \# recorded at training time if abs(current_mean_age - training_mean_age) \> 5: logging.warning(f'Potential drift: batch mean age {current_mean_age} vs training {training_mean_age}') \`\`\`                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          |

**Knowledge check:** Why is saving model artifacts with a version tag and training date preferable to always overwriting a single unversioned model.pkl file?

**(A) It lets you trace exactly which model version produced a given prediction and roll back if a retrained version performs worse**

\(B\) Versioned filenames make the model file size smaller

\(C\) scikit-learn refuses to load any file not named with a version tag

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Add model versioning (tagged filename with date) and one basic drift-check log statement to your capstone's deployment script.

**Lecture 620 deployment**

*Year 3 · Month 36 · Final Data Science & AI Capstone · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
|-------------------------|-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Deploy the capstone model as a working Streamlit (or FastAPI) demo and walk through a real test request and its output.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
| **Teacher explanation** | This lecture is the actual deployment build: wiring the saved, versioned model into a small interactive app that takes a patient record (or a selection from the test set) and returns the readmission risk score, the deployed threshold decision (flag / don't flag), and — using the interpretability chosen back in lecture 615 — the top 2-3 contributing features for that specific prediction. Walking through one real request end to end, from input to output to explanation, is what turns 'I trained a model' into 'I built something that works,' and it's the artifact that gets demoed live in interviews from Month 35. |
| **Worked example**      | \`\`\`python import streamlit as st st.title('Readmission Risk Checker (Capstone Demo)') prior_admissions = st.slider('Prior admissions', 0, 10, 2) age = st.slider('Age', 18, 100, 65) los = st.slider('Length of stay (days)', 1, 30, 4) score = model.predict_proba(\[\[prior_admissions, age, los\]\])\[0\]\[1\] st.write(f'Risk score: {score:.2f} -- {"FLAG for follow-up" if score \> 0.25 else "standard follow-up"}') st.write('Top factors: prior_admissions (+), age (+), length_of_stay (+)') \`\`\`                                                                                                                        |

**Knowledge check:** Why is walking through one complete real request (input through to the explained output) an important part of a capstone deployment lecture, beyond just writing the deployment code?

**(A) It proves the whole pipeline actually works end to end and produces the concrete artifact used to demo the project live, e.g. in an interview**

\(B\) It is required because Streamlit apps cannot be tested any other way

\(C\) Deployment code cannot be verified without a live internet connection

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Deploy your capstone model as a small interactive app (Streamlit or a minimal API) and run one real end-to-end test request, recording its output.

**Lecture 621 communication**

*Year 3 · Month 36 · Final Data Science & AI Capstone · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
|-------------------------|---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Structure the capstone's final deliverable into an executive summary, technical appendix, and repository, mirroring Month 35's portfolio standards at capstone scale.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               |
| **Teacher explanation** | The finished capstone deliverable has three layers for three different readers, same principle as Month 35's case study but now covering the full lifecycle: an executive summary (half a page — problem, headline finding, recommendation, with numbers, no code), a technical appendix (the methodology detail — pipeline design, EDA validation, model comparison, deployment choice — for a reviewer who wants to verify the rigor), and the repository itself (meeting every Month 35 repo-quality bar: clean structure, pinned dependencies, tests, no secrets, a passing CI badge). Each layer should stand on its own — a reader should get the headline from the summary alone without needing the appendix, and the appendix should let a skeptical technical reviewer verify every claim in the summary. |
| **Worked example**      | Executive summary opening: 'Patients with 3+ prior admissions are readmitted within 30 days at nearly 4x the rate of first-time patients (34% vs 9%, p\<0.001). A gradient-boosted risk model (recall 0.69 at a cost-weighted threshold) can flag the highest-risk 20% of discharges for prioritized care-coordination follow-up. Recommendation: pilot risk-based call prioritization for one quarter, re-measuring readmission rate in the flagged segment against a randomly-selected control group.' No code, no jargon, a specific recommendation with a built-in validation plan.                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |

**Knowledge check:** Why should the executive summary be readable and complete on its own, without requiring the reader to open the technical appendix?

**(A) Different readers need different depths, and a decision-maker should be able to get the headline finding and recommendation without wading through methodology**

\(B\) Executive summaries are a formatting requirement with no functional purpose

\(C\) Technical appendices are optional and most capstones should omit them entirely

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Write your capstone's executive summary (half a page, no code) so that it stands alone and leads directly to a specific recommendation.

**Lecture 622 communication**

*Year 3 · Month 36 · Final Data Science & AI Capstone · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                              |
|-------------------------|----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **Learning outcome**    | Prepare for a live capstone presentation to a mixed audience, including anticipated Q&A and defending specific modeling choices.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                             |
| **Teacher explanation** | Presenting a capstone live differs from writing it up: you must handle follow-up questions in real time, and the most common capstone Q&A questions are predictable — 'why this model and not a neural network,' 'how do you know this isn't overfit,' 'what would you do with more time,' 'what's a limitation of this approach.' Preparing specific, honest answers in advance (drawing on the model card from 617 and the explicit rationale from 615) turns a potentially rattling question into a moment that demonstrates judgment. A live demo (the Streamlit app from 620) should be rehearsed at least once end to end before presenting, including what to say if it breaks live — a calm 'let me show you the cached output while I check that' is far better than visible panic. |
| **Worked example**      | Pre-written answer to 'why not deep learning': 'I considered it, but with roughly 45,000 rows and a strong need for interpretability for the care coordination team, a gradient-boosted tree model gave comparable or better performance with explanations I could actually hand to a non-technical stakeholder — deep learning would have added complexity without a clear benefit here.' This is the same rationale from lecture 615, now rehearsed as a spoken answer rather than a written note.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |

**Knowledge check:** Why is it valuable to pre-write answers to predictable Q&A questions (like 'why not deep learning') before a live capstone presentation?

**(A) It lets you deliver a considered, specific answer under time pressure instead of improvising a weaker one in the moment**

\(B\) Presentations are graded solely on whether a script was read verbatim

\(C\) Audiences are not permitted to ask questions during a capstone presentation

***Correct answer: A***

**Homework:** Write out answers to at least three likely Q&A questions about your capstone, and rehearse your live demo once end to end before presenting.

**(A) A proven, audience-tested structure (problem, finding, method, demo, recommendation) transfers directly and reliably across different projects**

\(B\) Presentation software requires exactly five sections to render correctly

*Year 3 · Month 36 · Final Data Science & AI Capstone · 1 guided hour + homework*

|                         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |

| **Learning outcome**    | Complete the final examination of the 3-year, 624-lecture Data Science & AI Professional Program, reviewing the full arc from Python fundamentals to an independently built, deployed capstone.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| **Teacher explanation** | This final lecture closes a journey that began in lecture 1 with 'what is a variable' and ends here, 624 lectures later, with an independently scoped, built, validated, deployed, and presented machine learning project. Year 1 built the foundation: Python, SQL, statistics, pandas, visualization, EDA, and dashboarding, anchored by DP-900 and the Google Data Analytics certificate. Year 2 built modeling and engineering depth: supervised and unsupervised machine learning, feature engineering, time series, data engineering pipelines, Azure's AI-300 (the current successor to the retired DP-100), MLOps fundamentals, and the IBM Data Science and Data Engineering certificates. Year 3 built professional range: advanced ML, deep learning, NLP, computer vision, generative AI and RAG, data engineering at scale, experimentation, responsible AI, production MLOps, and finally this capstone trio — a real-world project, a genuine portfolio, and an independently built final capstone proving every one of those skills together on one problem, end to end, without a template to follow. As with every exam in this program, the internal passing bar is 80%; reaching it here specifically means your capstone's problem statement, pipeline, analysis, model, deployment, and presentation each independently meet the standards set across the preceding 623 lectures, not that you merely completed the activity. |
| **Worked example**      | Closing exam reflection exercise: trace one single decision in your finished capstone — the deployment threshold you chose in lecture 618-620 — all the way back through the skills that made it possible: the cost-weighted thinking first taught with the Lumen Retail churn model in Month 34, the precision/recall mechanics first taught in Month 15's classification unit back in Year 2, and the statistical validation habits first taught in Month 4-5's Statistics I and II in Year 1. No single lecture taught you to make that one deployment decision well — three years of accumulated, connected skill did. That is the real content of this final exam: not a new fact to learn, but the demonstrated ability to pull the right earlier lesson, from any point across three years, into a brand-new problem you were never shown before.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            |

**Knowledge check:** What is this final examination actually assessing, as described in this lecture?

**(A) Whether skills built across all three years can be integrated and applied independently to a new, previously unseen problem, not whether any single new fact was memorized**

\(B\) Whether the student can recite the full list of 624 lecture titles from memory

\(C\) Whether the student's capstone uses the exact same dataset as the Month 34 Lumen Retail project

***Correct answer: A***
